lessons.title: Maintenance & Servicing
lessons.objective: Describe scheduled and unscheduled maintenance; test compression and find where a cylinder leaks; list the steps of an overhaul and the care taken in taking an engine apart and putting a cylinder back; and set out how an engine is preserved, stored and returned to service.
lessons.purpose: Explain how engineers preserve the engine's performance, reliability and airworthiness.

steps.title: Scheduled and unscheduled maintenance
steps.prompt: Work on an engine is either planned or forced. Scheduled maintenance is on the maintenance program, is usually mandatory, and is preventive. Unscheduled maintenance is reactive: it follows a fault or an incident, is diagnostic or corrective, and is recorded as corrective action. The daily and preflight checks are the first line: oil level, leaks, visible damage, propeller security, induction and exhaust connections, and the mixture, throttle and carburettor heat linkages. Most engine defects come from poor lubrication, inadequate cooling, ignition or fuel faults, detonation or pre-ignition, improper maintenance, or wear and poor storage. Always work to the engine maker's manual and the aircraft handbook.
steps.note: Documented from the course deck (slides 248 and 249: scheduled versus unscheduled maintenance; the daily and preflight checks; the frequent causes of defects). The deck is the only source for this step, so its claims need the instructor's confirmation. The 2025-2026 daily quiz activity (days 6-7) asks which checks come first on a preflight inspection.

mediaPlan.rationale: A framing step: two kinds of maintenance and the usual causes of defects.

steps.title: Why an engine is maintained
steps.prompt:
Maintenance keeps an engine safe to fly and able to give the power it was certified to give. Its aims are airworthiness, reliability and performance.

An engine is not reliable by design alone. The manufacturer builds in reliability and durability and recommends a time between overhauls, but the handbook says continued reliability is determined by the maintenance, overhaul and operating personnel.

Preventive maintenance is the cheapest way to keep it. Regular checks, lubrication, cleaning and replacement on schedule find the oil leak, the worn plug or the low compression before they become a failure in flight.

The Tanzanian regulations put the duty on the owner or operator: they must maintain the aircraft in an airworthy condition, and an aircraft that is not may not be operated until it is restored.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 23 to 24 (reliability and durability; continued reliability is determined by maintenance, overhaul and operating personnel; the manufacturer specifies a recommended TBO) and the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026, regulation 21(1) (an owner or operator of an aircraft shall maintain the aircraft in an airworthy condition) and 22(2) (a failure to maintain an aircraft in an airworthy condition renders it ineligible for operation until restored). The three aims are the lesson's summary of the instructor's outcomes 1 and 17.

steps.title: Six words, six jobs
steps.prompt:
Technicians use these words exactly, and the records depend on them.

Inspection: examining an aircraft or component to establish that it conforms to a standard approved by the Authority.

Maintenance: the tasks needed to ensure continuing airworthiness, including overhaul, inspection, replacement, rectifying defects, and modifications or repairs.

Repair: restoring to an airworthy condition after damage or wear.

Overhaul: restoring using acceptable methods, including disassembly, cleaning, inspection, repair as necessary and reassembly.

Preventive maintenance: simple or minor preservation and replacing small standard parts.

Servicing is supplying the engine with oil, fuel and filters. Troubleshooting is working back from a symptom to its cause, as in the last lesson.

Choose the word that fits the job.
steps.note: Inspection, maintenance, repair, overhaul and preventive maintenance as the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026 define them, regulation 2. Servicing and troubleshooting are the course's working definitions: servicing from the Terminologies lesson, troubleshooting from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 403 (a systematic analysis of the symptoms that indicate engine malfunction). The wording above is shortened from the regulation.

steps.title: Follow the approved data
steps.prompt:
An engine is not maintained from memory or from a general book. The person doing the work must use the methods, techniques and practices in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness. If those are not available, they use methods the Authority has approved.

If the manufacturer recommends special tools or test equipment, they must be used, or an equivalent the Authority accepts.

The work must leave the engine at least equal to its original condition: in strength, resistance to vibration and deterioration, and the other qualities that affect airworthiness.

The handbook and this course teach the principles. The data for the engine in front of you gives the figures. A slide, an old manual or the manual of another variant is not approved data.
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026, regulation 30(1) to (3) (a person who performs maintenance shall use the methods, techniques and practices prescribed in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness, or methods approved by the Authority where the manufacturer's documents were not available; the special equipment the manufacturer recommends, or its equivalent; the work to be at least equal to the original or properly altered condition) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 369 (the technician should follow the manufacturer's manuals and information). The remark about slides and other variants is the lesson's, consistent with the Terminologies lesson on the -H variant.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Limits and tolerances
steps.prompt:
Every engine manual gives numbers that a part must stay within. A tolerance is the variation allowed from a nominal figure. A service limit is the most wear a part may have, or the least strength, and still be used.

Examples from the GTSIO-520 manuals: a new inner valve spring pushes back 78 to 88 lb at 1.329 in, and it is not reused if it gives less than 73 lb. The spark plug gap is 0.017 to 0.018 in. The cylinder hold-down nuts are torqued to 490 to 510 inch-pounds.

A part inside its limits goes back on. A part outside them is repaired, if the manual allows, or replaced.

Measure with the tools the manual names.

A reading that is only just inside a limit is worth noting, because the trend over several checks shows wear building up.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 95 (page B-4, spring test data: inner spring 78 to 88 lb new and 73 lb serviceable limit at 1.329 in), PDF p. 100 (the torque table: cylinder hold-down nuts, 7/16-20, 490 to 510 inch-pounds, 40.8 to 42.5 foot-pounds) and PDF p. 153 (page C-3-3, spark plug gap 0.017 to 0.018 in) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 369 (each manufacturer provides very specific tolerances to which the parts must conform; the manufacturer publishes a new minimum and serviceable dimension for critical parts). The figures are teaching data from a 1980/1981 manual edition, not a maintenance instruction. The tools named by the manual: the Tanzanian regulation 30(1)(d) requires the tools, equipment and test apparatus necessary to complete the work to accepted industry practice.

steps.title: The outside inspection
steps.prompt:
A great deal of an engine's health can be read from outside, with the cowling off and a good light. An external inspection looks at:

Leaks: oil, fuel and coolant at joints, hoses, gaskets and fittings.

Security: nuts, bolts, clamps and hoses, the engine mount, the propeller, and the safety wire and cotter pins.

Induction and exhaust: connections, clamps, gaskets and cracks.

Controls: throttle, mixture and carburettor heat, with free and full travel.

The propeller: splits and chips.

Baffles, cowling and fins: damage, blockage and missing parts.

The ignition harness and wiring: chafing, cracks and loose terminals.

Always work through the engine in the same order, so that nothing is skipped.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 455 (a light-sport engine preflight list: inspect the engine and gearbox for oil leaks; loose or missing nuts, bolts and screws; security of the engine mounting; the air filter and intake silencer; the spark plug connectors; the propeller for splits and chips) and the opening step of this lesson (the daily and preflight checks: oil level, leaks, visible damage, propeller security, induction and exhaust connections, and linkages). Exhaust leaks and inspection: PDF p. 150. The list is a general example; the aircraft's own maintenance manual gives the actual list.

steps.title: Reading the evidence
steps.prompt:
The handbook has exact words for what an inspector sees. Use them, because the record must.

Corrosion: loss of metal by chemical action. Rust is an example.

Chafing: wear from two parts rubbing under light pressure.

Burning: surface damage from excessive heat, from a poor fit, poor lubrication or running too hot. It shows as discoloured or blistered metal and paint.

Crack: a partial separation of material, from vibration, overloading or fatigue.

Dent, nick and gouge: damage from blows or careless handling.

Fretting and scoring: wear from small movements, or from particles between parts.

A leak shows as a wet streak, or a flat grey or sooty black one at an exhaust joint. Looseness shows as movement or a fastener out of its safety wire.

Each sign is evidence to record and follow up.
steps.note: Defect terms (corrosion, chafing, burning, crack, dent, nick, gouge, fretting and scoring) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 371 (terms used to describe defects detected during inspection). Exhaust leaks showing as flat grey or sooty black streaks and black soot around a failed gasket: PDF p. 150 and the Induction and Exhaust lesson. The description of looseness and wet streaks is the lesson's wording.

steps.title: The differential compression test
steps.prompt: A cylinder that leaks cannot make full power, so compression is tested at intervals and the results are recorded. Do it as soon as possible after the engine is shut down, while the rings and walls are still oiled. The ignition is off, and each plug is labelled to its cylinder. The tester feeds air at a regulated 80 psi through a small orifice into the cylinder, with the piston at top dead centre on compression. The cylinder gauge shows how much of the air stays in. If it reads less than the minimum for that engine, the cylinder is leaking.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of a differential compression tester: an air supply from a compressor passes a regulator with a regulated pressure gauge, a shutoff valve and a metering orifice, then a cylinder pressure gauge, into a cylinder whose piston is on true top dead centre.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 407-408 (the compression test shows whether the valves, rings and pistons seal the chamber; perform it as soon as possible after shutdown so the rings and walls are still lubricated; ignition off, plugs identified with their cylinders; the differential pressure tester measures leakage through the cylinder; set the regulator to 80 psi; the piston is brought up on compression to top dead centre; a reading below the minimum for the engine means low compression; Figure 10-53). The minimum reading is the manufacturer's figure and is not given here.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook's diagram shows the two gauges and the orifice that make the test a measure of leakage.

steps.title: Finding the leak
steps.prompt: A low reading says a cylinder leaks, not where. Listen while the test air is on. Air escaping at the exhaust outlet is leaking past the exhaust valve. Air escaping at the air intake is leaking past the intake valve. Air coming out of the crankcase breather is leaking past the piston and rings. Next to the valves, the piston is the most common cause, and a lack of oil is one reason, so put oil in the cylinder and test again. If a valve is the cause, check its clearance. If the pressure is still low, the cylinder is replaced. Record every reading, because the trend across checks shows wear building up.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 408-409 (cylinders below the minimum are checked further: leakage past the exhaust valve at the exhaust outlet, the intake valve at the air intake, the piston rings at the breather outlets; next to valve blow-by, the most frequent cause of compression leakage is leakage past the piston, which can be a lack of oil; apply oil and re-check, and replace the cylinder if still below the minimum) and PDF p. 407 (records of previous checks show progressive wear; check valve clearance; if blow-by remains, replace the cylinder). The course deck (slide 257) asks the same question as a recap.

mediaPlan.rationale: Three leak paths and the three places to listen; the learner matches them in a check.

steps.title: Oil, filters and screens
steps.prompt:
Engine oil lubricates, cools, seals and cleans, and it carries away evidence of wear. So it is changed on a schedule and read as a record.

The oil filter removes solid particles before they reach the bearings. Aircraft filters are of four types: screen, Cuno, canister and spin-on, and the full-flow spin-on is the most widely used. A screen is cleaned at regular intervals, and a paper element is replaced. A bypass valve lets unfiltered oil through if the filter clogs, since dirty oil is better than no lubrication.

At an oil change: drain the oil, strain it or look at it for metal, examine the filter element and screens for metal particles, then refill with the right oil to the right level.

Metal in the oil or on the filter is a warning, and if it is found an overhaul may be indicated.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 252 to 253 (the engine oil pump and filter; the four filter types: screen, Cuno, canister and spin-on; full-flow spin-on filters are the most widely used; the bypass valve; dirty oil in an engine is better than no lubrication; screens cleaned at regular intervals), PDF p. 370 (drain the oil, strain it through a clean cloth and check the cloth and the filter for metal particles) and PDF pp. 404 to 405 (metal particles in the sump: overhaul indicated). Cleaning fuel and oil strainers is preventive maintenance under the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026, regulation 29(w).

steps.title: Servicing spark plugs
steps.prompt:
Spark plugs are removed for servicing at the manufacturer's intervals, and sooner if a fault is traced to one.

Handle each plug alone, and keep it in a tray labelled by cylinder. A plug dropped on a hard floor is discarded: the insulator may be cracked where it cannot be seen.

Inspect first: the threads, the lead barrel for corrosion and cracks, and the firing end for cracked or chipped insulator and worn electrodes. Clean the plugs that pass, with a vibrator cleaner and an abrasive blast, never by soaking. Set the gap with a round wire gauge, since a flat gauge misreads, and test the plug under pressure. On the GTSIO-520-H the gap is 0.017 to 0.018 in.

Before fitting, clean the bushing and the seat. Use anti-seize sparingly, since graphite on the electrodes shorts the plug. Fit by hand, then torque as the manual says.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 194 to 197 (plugs removed at the manufacturer's intervals; handle individually; the tray; a dropped plug is discarded; visual inspection first; cleaning by vibrator cleaner and abrasive blast; do not soak in solvent; the plug tested under pressure; the gap checked with a round wire-thickness gauge, because a flat gauge gives an incorrect indication; graphite antiseize compound must not touch the electrodes; start the plug by hand, then torque to the specified value) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 153 (spark plug gap 0.017 to 0.018 in). Under the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026, regulation 29(t), replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap is preventive maintenance.

steps.title: The right fluid, the right amount
steps.prompt:
Servicing means giving the engine the right fluids, in the right amount, with nothing in them that should not be there.

Oil: use the grade the manufacturer gives. For the GTSIO-520-H that is SAE 50 above 40 °F, and 10W30 multigrade or SAE 30 below, with a sump capacity of 13 quarts. Check the level on the dipstick, a bayonet gauge, before flight. A new engine may carry a preservative oil that is removed at the first 25 hours, and until then only the oils the manufacturer allows may be added.

Fuel: use the grade the manual gives. The GTSIO-520-H takes 100LL (blue) or 100 (green) aviation gasoline, and a lower grade can cause detonation.

A wrong fluid, a wrong amount or a contaminated one can ruin an engine, so note what was added.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (the -H: oil SAE No. 50 above 40 degrees F and 10W30 multi-viscosity or SAE No. 30 below; oil sump capacity 13 quarts; fuel, aviation grade, 100LL (blue) or 100 (green)) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 250 (preservative oil removed at the end of the first 25 hours of operation; use only the oils allowed while it is in the engine) and PDF p. 252 (the dipstick-type quantity gauge, often called a bayonet gauge). That a lower grade can cause detonation: the High compression and fuel step of Power Generation.

steps.title: Where the other inspections live
steps.prompt:
Four more inspections belong to the lessons that taught the parts.

The valve train (lesson 8): valves are checked for a worn face and tip, stretch, burning and a thin margin. A spring that pushes back with less than its limit is not reused, and hydraulic tappets are checked for damaged faces and for a plunger that does not kick back.

The exhaust (lesson 11): clamps, welds and gaskets are checked for leaks and cracks, because an exhaust failure can mean carbon monoxide, power loss or fire.

The reasons are simple. A worn valve or weak spring loses compression. A failed tappet spoils the valve timing. A cracked exhaust is a safety hazard.

The practical sessions repeat these checks on real engines.
steps.note: Pointers to the Valve Operating lesson (inspecting a valve, checking a valve spring, the camshaft and tappets: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 379 to 384, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 66 to 67 and 95) and the Induction and Exhaust lesson (inspecting the exhaust: PDF pp. 149 to 151). The instructor's outcomes 11 to 14 for this lesson are taught there; this step only places them in the maintenance round.

steps.title: When an engine comes off
steps.prompt: An engine is removed when it cannot be inspected or repaired where it is, or when it reaches a limit: it is due for overhaul, it has lost performance, it leaks heavily, a major part has failed, or it has corroded in storage. After a propeller strike or a sudden stop it is removed for internal checks. Once it is off, it is taken apart for a reason: metal in the oil, lost compression, detonation damage, internal corrosion, odd noises, crankshaft runout, or an airworthiness directive or service bulletin that needs it. One faulty part can still mean a full teardown. A first check on any engine for complete overhaul is the runout of the crankshaft or propeller shaft.
steps.note: Documented from the course deck (slide 250, reasons for engine removal; slide 252, reasons for disassembly) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 370 (any engine to be completely overhauled should first have its crankshaft or propeller shaft runout checked, and a shaft beyond its limits must be replaced; service bulletins are not mandatory unless an airworthiness directive refers to them or the inspection program requires them). The deck says that a propeller strike or hard landing makes engine removal mandatory; the handbook text read here does not say so, and the lesson keeps the wording to a reason for internal checks.

mediaPlan.rationale: A list of reasons the learner will meet again in the course's practical work.

steps.title: Overhaul and time before overhaul
steps.prompt: Each manufacturer sets a total time in service, in hours, at which an engine is overhauled. The handbook calls it the time before overhaul, TBO, and the course deck calls it time between overhauls. Depending on how the engine is used, it can be mandatory. A top overhaul reconditions only the parts above the crankcase, such as the cylinders, pistons, rings and valve gear, without dismantling the engine, and is really a repair. A major overhaul is a complete reconditioning. It has ten steps: receiving inspection, disassembly, visual inspection, cleaning, structural inspection, non-destructive testing, dimensional inspection, repair and replacement, reassembly, and testing and break-in.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 369 (overhaul is set by the manufacturer's recommended hours, called time before overhaul, TBO, and depending on use it can be mandatory; an engine with a life of 2,000 hours that has operated 500 hours has 1,500 hours remaining; a complete overhaul has ten steps; a top overhaul is an overhaul of the parts above the crankcase without completely dismantling the engine, is really a repair and not a true overhaul; a major overhaul is the complete reconditioning of the powerplant). EASA Module 16, PDF p. 334 (Figure 14-1) and the course deck (slide 265) call it time between overhaul.

mediaPlan.rationale: One list the learner has to be able to say in order; an ordering check tests it.

steps.title: Taking the engine apart
steps.prompt: Start with the paperwork: the engine's history, its service bulletins and airworthiness directives. Then mount it on an overhaul stand and clean the outside. During disassembly, drain the oil and strain it through a clean cloth, and look at the cloth and the filter for metal. Lay every part out in order, with a container for small parts, so that visual inspection can follow at once. Tag loose studs and damaged fittings. Use the right tool, not a makeshift one. Throw away every safety device as it comes out: lockwire, cotter pins, tab washers, seals and gaskets are never used a second time. Do not clean the engine with a caustic solution, which can strip the finish.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 370 (receiving inspection and records review; the engine is mounted on an overhaul stand; drain the oil and strain it through a clean cloth and check for metal particles; lay parts out in an orderly manner; tag loose studs and damaged fittings; use the proper tool; never reuse safety wire or cotter pins) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 55 (paragraphs 7-3 to 7-5: discard shakeproof washers, lockwires, tab washers, seals, gaskets, cotter pins and hose connectors; use a tilting-bed stand; do not use a caustic or alkaline cleaner, which removes the alodized finish of some aluminium parts). Chapter A is written for the basic GTSIO-520; check the -H difference data in Chapter C-3 for any change.

mediaPlan.rationale: Practical habits listed once; the 3D cylinder in the rest of the course already shows the parts.

steps.title: Taking a cylinder off
steps.prompt: First, turn the crankshaft so the piston is at top dead centre on compression, which frees the rocker arms, and take out the pushrods. Mark each so it can go back where it came from. Take off all the hold-down nuts except two, 180° apart, then support the cylinder and take off the last two. Pull it straight out along the studs, and catch the piston as it clears the barrel. Before the piston comes out, put a cloth in the opening so no piece of a broken ring falls into the crankcase. When the cylinder is off, support the connecting rod: the base seal ring looped round the rod and the studs will do. The manual may call for a wooden block under the cylinder when removing the valve springs.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 409-410 (turn the crankshaft to top dead centre on compression to relieve the rocker arms before removing the pushrods; mark the pushrods; remove all but two nuts 180 degrees apart; support the cylinder, with two technicians; a cloth stops pieces of broken rings falling into the crankcase; the connecting rod must be supported after removal, by the removed cylinder base oil seal ring looped around the rod and the base studs) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 57-58 (paragraph 7-15: the cylinder is withdrawn straight outward and the piston caught as it clears; a cylindrical wood block is recommended for removing the valve springs). The deck (slides 253 and 257) says wooden supports or rubber collars on the rods.

mediaPlan.rationale: A sequence of actions the learner follows in order.

steps.title: Inspect before you clean
steps.prompt: The first inspection is visual and it comes before cleaning, because the residual deposits of metal in the recesses of the engine can show how it failed. Then each part is checked in three ways: visual, structural and dimensional. Visual and structural checks look for defects such as cracks, with a bright light and a magnifier, with magnetic particle inspection for magnetic parts, or with dye penetrant, eddy current, ultrasound or X-ray. Dimensional checks measure each part against the manufacturer's limits. Some signs link back to what you have learned: a depression in the top of a piston usually means that detonation has occurred, and interior cracks in a cylinder head radiate from the valve seat or spark plug bosses.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 371 (visual inspection precedes all other procedures; parts should not be cleaned before a preliminary visual inspection because residual deposits of metallic particles may show a failure), PDF p. 370 (visual, structural and dimensional inspection; magnetic particle inspection for magnetic parts, and dye penetrant, eddy current, ultrasound and X-ray), PDF p. 372 (cylinder head interior cracks almost always radiate from the valve seat bosses or spark plug bushing boss) and PDF p. 373 (a depression in the top of the piston usually means that detonation has occurred).

mediaPlan.rationale: Ties the inspection back to the malfunctions lesson.

steps.title: Putting a cylinder back
steps.prompt: Oil the piston and rings, and place the ring gaps as the manual says. For the GTSIO-520 the gaps of alternate rings sit 180° apart. Put the piston on the rod with its number toward the front. Compress the rings with a ring compressor and ease the cylinder on straight and without rocking, or a ring can escape and break. Fit two nuts 180° apart, then the rest, snug. Then torque them to the manual's value, in the manual's sequence, with a slow, steady pull, and safety them. Put the pushrods back in their own places, not turned end for end, and set the valve clearance.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 410-411 (oil the piston and stagger the ring gaps; compress the rings with a ring compressor and ease the cylinder on without rocking; install two nuts 180 degrees apart, then the rest snug; torque to the manufacturer's value with a slow, steady motion, then safety; pushrods go back in their original locations and must not be turned end to end; set the valve clearance), and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 75 (paragraph 11-8: the gaps of alternate rings are positioned 180 degrees apart), PDF p. 79-80 (paragraph 12-7: ring compressor, tighten the nuts moderately, torque in the sequence of Figure A-4-38) and PDF p. 100 (Table 2, cylinder hold-down nuts 7/16-20 at 490-510 inch-pounds, 40.8-42.5 foot-pounds). The course deck (slide 254) gives a 120 degree stagger and a ring end gap of 0.015 to 0.030 in; neither is in the handbook or the manual read here, and this lesson follows the manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: A sequence of actions and one torque value; the learner converts units in a check.

steps.title: Why engines are preserved
steps.prompt: An engine that sits does not stay as it was. Combustion leaves moisture and corrosive by-products that attack the cylinder walls and valves, and with no flying and no daily attention nothing removes them. Engines near the sea, lakes, rivers or in humid regions are at greater risk. Running the engine on the ground is not the answer. Each shutdown leaves water in the crankcase, and only a flight that holds the oil at about 180°F for at least 30 minutes drives it out. A ground run does not, so repeated ground runs build up water in the oil and make corrosion worse. That is why preservation is a procedure with steps and a record.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 345 (an engine awaiting overhaul or return to service does not receive the daily attention needed to catch early corrosion; combustion creates moisture and corrosive by-products that attack unprotected cylinder walls, valves and other surfaces; engines near oceans, lakes, rivers and humid regions have a greater need for preservation) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 323 (running the engine on the ground is harmful: water from each shutdown is purged only by operating at least 30 minutes at 180 degrees F, which ground runs do not achieve, so water accumulates and causes corrosion). The course deck (slide 264) asks the same question as a recap.

mediaPlan.rationale: The reason for preservation, and the surprising point about ground runs.

steps.title: Three levels of storage
steps.prompt: The longer an engine will sit, the more is done to it. In active storage the engine has had at least an hour of continuous running with the oil at 165 to 200°F, and not more than 30 days pass. The EASA text calls this flyable storage. Temporary storage is for an aircraft that is not flown for 30 to 90 days. Indefinite storage is for over 90 days, or for an engine removed from the aircraft for a long time. In indefinite storage the preservative is renewed at least every six months. The course deck divides storage differently, as up to 30 days, one to six months, and over six months. The handbook and the EASA text agree on 30 and 90 days, and the lesson follows them.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 345 (three types of storage: active, with at least one continuous hour of operation at an oil temperature of at least 165 to 200 degrees F and not more than 30 days; temporary, 30 to 90 days; indefinite, over 90 days or removed from the aircraft for an extended time) and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 323-326 (flyable, temporary storage limited to 90 days, and indefinite storage for over 90 days; preservation renewed every six months). The course deck (slide 259) groups storage as short term up to 30 days, medium term 1-6 months and long term over 6 months, and its slide 264 as flyable up to 30 days and temporary or indefinite beyond; the handbook and EASA text are followed here and the deck needs the instructor's confirmation.

mediaPlan.rationale: Three levels set out by duration; a matching check tests them.

steps.title: Preserving an engine
steps.prompt: Run the engine until it is at normal temperature for at least an hour, drain the oil, and refill with a preservative oil. The GTSIO-520 manual specifies MIL-C-6529 Type II, preheated to 225°F. Remove the spark plugs. Spray each cylinder with preservative through the plug hole with the piston at bottom centre, then spray each again with no piston at top centre. Then do not turn the crankshaft, because that would scrape off the coating, and fit a placard saying so, with the date. Fit dehydrator plugs. Spray and seal the exhaust ports and the intake, put silica gel in the intake, and write down every seal and plug.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 345-347 (before temporary or indefinite storage, operate the engine until normal temperature for at least an hour and replace the oil with a preservative mixture; remove the plug leads and top plugs; spray each cylinder at bottom center and again with no piston at top dead center; the crankshaft must not be moved after the last spraying, the seal would be broken, and a sign reads DO NOT TURN CRANKSHAFT, ENGINE PRESERVED, with the date; dehydrator plugs in the plug holes; the exhaust ports are sprayed and sealed; the intake is sealed with silica gel bags), EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 324-325 (the placard, the sealing of ports, and the list of what was plugged) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 54 (paragraph 6-3: oil sump filled to the full mark with MIL-C-6529 Type II, which must be preheated to 225 degrees F; the engine is run first, and stored longer than about a week). The 225 degrees F is the manufacturer's value for that product and engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: The steps are easiest to remember as one sequence; the learner states the order in the last step.

steps.title: Reading the dehydrator plugs
steps.prompt: A dehydrator plug is a clear plug holding silica gel treated with cobalt chloride, screwed into a spark plug hole. It is also a humidity gauge. Bright blue means the air in the engine is dry, below 30 percent relative humidity, where corrosion does not normally take place. As the humidity rises it fades to lavender at about 30 percent, then through the pinks, to white at 60 percent. Pink means the plug has taken up moisture. Look at them every 15 days in indefinite storage. Replace any that has changed colour, and if half or more have changed, replace all of the desiccant. Look into the cylinders, and if there is corrosion, spray and turn the engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 346 (the cobalt-chloride silica gel is bright blue at low relative humidity, lavender at 30 percent, through shades of pink to white at 60 percent; when the relative humidity is below 30 percent, corrosion does not normally take place; some types can be dried and returned to blue) and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 325-326 (blue is dry and pink means exposure to high moisture; engines in indefinite storage are inspected every 15 days; a plug that changes colour is replaced and, if half or more change, all the desiccants; if cylinder corrosion is found it is sprayed and the engine turned at least 10 turns). The course deck (slide 264) asks what the blue-to-pink change means.

mediaPlan.rationale: The colour code is the content; a matching check covers it.

steps.title: Returning to service
steps.prompt: Take off all the seals and the desiccant bags, and the dehydrator plugs. Drain the preservative oil from the sump, put the drain plug back, torque and safety it, change the filter, and service the engine with oil. Before you move the propeller, disconnect all the plug leads, make sure the magneto switches are off and the throttle closed, and stay out of the arc of the blades. Turn it by hand several revolutions to clear the preservative oil, and pre-oil the engine so that it makes oil pressure at the first start. Then fit plugs and leads, inspect, start, run the operational test and correct any faults. Change the oil and filter after 25 hours.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 347-348 (return to service: remove seals and desiccant bags; remove the dehydrator plugs; drain the preservative oil, torque and safety the drain plug, change the filter and service with oil; the warning to disconnect plug leads, check the magneto switches off, close the throttle, mixture to idle cut-off, and keep out of the arc before moving the propeller; rotate by hand several revolutions to clear preservative oil; install plugs and leads; inspect and correct; start and test; change the oil and filter after 25 hours) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 327 (pre-oiling before starting an engine that has been inactive, and after assembly) with the course deck (slide 263).

mediaPlan.rationale: A return-to-service sequence with its safety warning.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.prompt:
A job is not finished until it is recorded. The record is how the next technician, the owner and the Authority know the true condition of the engine.

In Tanzania each engine has its own log book, separate from the aircraft's. When the work has been done properly, the person who did it makes an entry saying what was done, or referring to the data they used; the engine's total time in service and its time since overhaul; the state of compliance with mandatory continuing airworthiness information such as airworthiness directives; and any modifications and repairs. The signature is the approval for return to service, for the work done and no more.

Entries are made promptly, and log books are kept for two years after the engine is destroyed or withdrawn.

If it was not recorded, it cannot be shown to have been done.
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzania Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, GN 57 of 2017, Revised Edition 2026, regulation 41 (a separate log book for each engine; entries made as soon as practicable after the occurrence, and not more than seven days after the expiry of the certificate of release to service; an entry on each occasion of maintenance, overhaul, repair, replacement, modification or inspection of the engine; kept for two years after the engine is destroyed or permanently withdrawn; a clear record of continued compliance with mandatory airworthiness requirements), regulation 42 (the maintenance record entry: a description of the work or a reference to data acceptable to the Authority; total time in service and time since overhaul; status of compliance with mandatory continuing airworthiness information; details of modifications and repairs; the signature approves return to service only for the work performed; a major repair is recorded on a prescribed form) and regulation 21(1)(c) to (d) (the certificate of release to service; open discrepancies listed). FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 369: complete records of the inspection process are kept with the engine records. The last sentence is the lesson's.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Plan a job
steps.prompt:
A six-cylinder engine is going to sit for four months while the aircraft is repaired, and you are told to make sure it comes out as good as it went in. Say in your own words which level of storage it needs, and why.

Then list, in order, what you would do to the engine to preserve it, what you would do to the plugs and ports, what you would check and how often while it sits, and what you would do when it returns to service. Say what you would write in the engine's log book, and whose data you would work to.

Finish by naming the one thing you must never do to the crankshaft in storage, and why.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the storage and preservation sequence (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 345-348, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 323-327. A four-month storage is temporary or indefinite storage depending on whether it passes 90 days; the deck would call it medium term.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner plans the job in their own words from what they have read.

lessons.title: Light Sport Aircraft
lessons.objective: Describe what makes an aircraft light-sport and why its engine must be light and reliable, name who may maintain and inspect these engines, recognise the common two-stroke and four-stroke light-sport engines, and carry out the basic checks and troubleshooting the handbook describes.
lessons.purpose: Give students a glimpse of the wider world of piston-powered aviation and introduce regulatory awareness.
outcomes: Explain broadly what is meant by light-sport and recreational aircraft.
Recognise that light aircraft may employ engines and installation philosophies different from conventional certified training aircraft.
Identify representative engines used in light and recreational aircraft.
Compare broad characteristics such as engine mass, cooling method, operating RPM, gearing and installation.
Explain why some light-aircraft engines operate at significantly different RPM ranges from conventional direct-drive aircraft engines.
Appreciate the role of piston engines in recreational flying, sport aviation, experimental aircraft and aircraft ownership.
Recognise that aircraft category and regulatory status can affect permissible maintenance activity.
Explain why an engineer must determine the applicable regulatory framework and maintenance privileges before carrying out maintenance.
Recognise that maintenance privileges may differ between conventional certified aircraft and some recreational/light-aircraft categories.
lessons.syllabusNote: This is enrichment rather than a requirement explicitly stated in the supplied AMT 4212G description, so the regulatory material should ultimately be anchored to the applicable Tanzanian/TCAA framework rather than assumed from another jurisdiction.
lessons.completionCriteria: Say what light-sport and recreational aircraft are, where the Tanzanian regulations place microlight and amateur-built aircraft, and why piston engines suit them; tell the common engines apart and say why some turn far faster than a conventional engine and use a gearbox; explain how the category and certificate of an aircraft, and the licence a person holds, decide what maintenance may be done and signed for, and say what to find out before working on one; work out an overhaul limit and a leak-down loss, read a spark plug tip and a magnetic plug, and describe the first action for an over-temperature or a knocking engine.

steps.title: What makes an aircraft light-sport
steps.prompt:
'Light-sport' is a category with limits. In the FAA handbook an aircraft qualifies by thirteen limits, among them a maximum takeoff weight of 1,320 lb (600 kg), a top speed of 120 knots at maximum continuous power, a stall speed of 45 knots or less, two seats at most, one reciprocating engine if powered, a fixed or ground-adjustable propeller, an unpressurized cabin and fixed landing gear. The handbook warns that regulations change.

Other words cover the same ground: ultralight, microlight, recreational, sport, kit-built, amateur-built and experimental. The words and the limits differ from state to state.

Tanzania's airworthiness regulations name microlight, experimental amateur-built and kit-built aircraft among those that may not qualify for a normal certificate. Why do you think engine weight and simplicity matter so much for them?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 434 (the thirteen requirements of a light-sport aircraft: maximum takeoff weight 1,320 lb or 1,430 lb for water, VH not more than 120 knots CAS, stall speed VS1 not more than 45 knots CAS, no more than two seats, a single reciprocating engine if powered, a fixed or ground-adjustable propeller, a non-pressurized cabin, fixed landing gear; the note that regulations are subject to change) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 333 (the same list). The course deck (slide 268) gives the stall limit as Vs0; the handbook says VS1, and the lesson follows the handbook. The Tanzanian airworthiness regulations, regulation 16, name microlight, experimental amateur and kit built aircraft (read 13 October 2026). No separate Tanzanian light-sport definition was found in the regulations, advisory circulars and rules read from the TCAA website; the instructor should confirm whether TCAA has a current circular on light-sport or recreational aircraft.

mediaPlan.rationale: The list of limits is the content; the numeric checks test the key figures.

steps.title: Who flies them, and why
steps.prompt:
Piston engines power almost all recreational aviation. People fly for pleasure, for sport and racing, to build an aircraft from a kit or from plans, and to own and look after an aircraft of their own.

The handbook says small general aviation aircraft use mostly horizontally opposed piston engines. For the lightest aircraft the engines are smaller still, and the aim is low weight, simplicity and low running cost.

Tanzania's regulations make room for this flying. A microlight, an experimental amateur-built or kit-built aircraft, an air-race or exhibition aircraft and a kite can be given a restricted certificate of airworthiness, with operating limitations.

Owners also take an interest in the engine itself, which is why the rules say what an owner or pilot may and may not do.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 22 (small general aviation aircraft use mostly horizontally opposed reciprocating piston engines) and PDF p. 434 (light-sport aircraft and their engines) and the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, regulation 16 (the Authority may issue a restricted certificate of airworthiness to an aircraft that does not qualify for a certificate of airworthiness including microlight, experimental amateur and kit built aircraft, an aircraft used for air races, aircraft flying for exhibition purpose and a kite; subject to operating limitations within the United Republic). The reasons people fly and the engineering aims (low weight, simplicity, low running cost) are the lesson's summary of the instructor's outcome 6, with the handbook's emphasis on weight and reliability in the next step.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Engines for a narrow margin
steps.prompt: Light-sport aircraft have a narrow margin of useful load, so every excess pound of engine reduces performance. Weight is a key concern. The engine must also be reliable: able to deliver its rating in all flight attitudes and in extreme weather. Its maker ensures this by design, research and testing. Most of these engines are not FAA-certificated, but their makers keep a close control of manufacture and assembly, test every engine before it leaves the factory, and meet American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) standards. Some engines used in light-sport aircraft are FAA-certificated, and they are maintained to the maker's instructions and 14 CFR.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 434 (light-sport aircraft have a narrow margin of useful load; engine weight is very important; reliability means performing at the specified ratings in widely varying attitudes and extreme weather; most of these engines are not certificated by the FAA but are closely controlled, factory tested and meet ASTM standards; some are FAA-certificated and are maintained per the manufacturer's instructions and 14 CFR) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 333. The course deck (slide 271) divides engines into certified engines designed under ASTM standards and experimental engines; the handbook does not describe the Continental O-200 that way and the lesson does not either.

mediaPlan.rationale: Two ideas, weight and how reliability is assured when most engines are not certificated.

steps.title: Overhaul time and calendar life
steps.prompt: Most light-sport engines need an overhaul after a set time. The maker sets or implies it, and it depends on the type of engine, the engine temperatures, the time spent at high power, and the maintenance given. The table shows the handbook's examples for the Rotax 914. Each limit is in hours and in years, and whichever comes first ends the engine's life. For the earlier engines, carrying out service bulletin SB-914-027 can raise the limit to between 1,000 and 1,200 hours, or 12 years. A seldom-flown engine can reach its calendar limit long before its hours. After that limit the engine is overhauled, sometimes at the maker's facility.
steps.alt: FAA table, Examples of TBO and calendar life for engines. Rotax 914 F and 914 UL engines up to a given serial number have a time between overhaul of 1,000 hours or 10 years whichever comes first, which service bulletin SB-914-027 can raise to 1,000 to 1,200 hours or 12 years. Later engines have 1,200 hours or 12 years, whichever comes first, and need no bulletin.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 434-435 (most light-sport engines require a definite time interval between overhauls, specified or implied by the manufacturer; it varies with the type of engine, operating conditions such as engine temperatures, time at high-power settings, and the maintenance received; after the limit the engine has to be overhauled, sometimes at an authorized manufacturer's facility; Figure 11-1, examples of TBO and calendar life for engines). EASA Module 16, PDF p. 334 has the same table. The figures are examples for those serial numbers, not general limits.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook table shows hours and calendar limits together.

steps.title: Why some engines turn so fast
steps.prompt:
Small engines make their power by turning fast. The HKS 700T, a flat twin of 709 cc, makes 80 hp at 5,300 rpm and weighs 126 lb.

A propeller cannot follow. When its blade tips approach the speed of sound its efficiency falls rapidly. So an engine that turns fast drives the propeller through a reduction gearbox. The HKS 700T's gearbox has a ratio of 2.13 to 1, so the propeller turns at 5,300 ÷ 2.13, about 2,490 rpm.

Engines that run slower can drive the propeller directly. The Jabiru 2200 makes 85 hp at 3,300 rpm and the Continental O-200 100 hp at 2,750 rpm, both with direct drive. The handbook says the direct drive keeps the Jabiru light and its maintenance costs low.

The gearbox is the trade: more weight and more parts for a faster, lighter engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 442 (the HKS 700T: four-stroke, two cylinder, turbocharged, intercooled, 709 cc, a reduction gearbox driving the propeller flange at a speed reduction ratio of 2.13 to 1, rated at 77 horsepower continuous and 80 horsepower takeoff (3 minutes) at 4,900 rpm and 5,300 rpm, total engine weight 126 pounds), PDF p. 44 (reduction gearing limits the propeller rotation speed; when blade tips approach the speed of sound the efficiency decreases rapidly), PDF p. 443 (the Jabiru: direct crankshaft drive without a reduction gearbox facilitates its lightweight design and keeps maintenance costs to a minimum) and PDF pp. 443 to 445 (Jabiru 2200: 85 hp at 3,300 rpm; Continental O-200: 100 bhp at 2,750 rpm). The propeller speed is the quotient; see also Accessories and Drives.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Two-stroke engines: Rotax 503 and 582
steps.prompt: Many light-sport aircraft and ultralights fly with the Rotax 447, 503 or 582: a two-cylinder, two-stroke inline engine with a small frontal area. It is piston ported. The 447 and 503 are air-cooled, and the 582 is liquid-cooled, with a water pump, a radiator, a pressure cap and an overflow bottle. As a two-stroke engine it must be lubricated by oil in the fuel, either premixed at 1:50, which is 2 percent oil, or from an oil tank by an injection pump driven from the crankshaft. The pump's delivery follows engine speed and a lever linked to the throttle. Ignition is a breakerless capacitor discharge system, and the propeller is driven through a gearbox with a shock absorber.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 436-438 (the Rotax 447 UL SCDI and 503 UL DCDI two-cylinder inline two-stroke, piston ported, fan or free air-cooled; the 582 liquid-cooled, with pressure cap and overflow bottle; lubrication by oil premixed in the fuel at 1:50 (2 percent) or oil injection from a separate tank by a crankshaft-driven pump whose output follows rpm and the throttle-linked lever; breakerless capacitor discharge ignition, a dual system on the 503 and single on the 447; a flange-connected gearbox with shock absorber). The handbook says its light-sport maintenance notes are for education and not for actual maintenance: the current manufacturer's instructions always apply. The course deck (slide 272) lists the Rotax 582 as a liquid-cooled inline two-cylinder.

mediaPlan.rationale: A compact description of the two-stroke line; the learner has met two-strokes in the Thermodynamic Cycles lesson.

steps.title: The four-stroke flat four: Rotax 914
steps.prompt: The Rotax 912 and 914 are four-cylinder, four-stroke horizontally opposed engines. They weigh about the same as the 582, have a narrow outline and low vibration, and are ASTM approved for light-sport aircraft, with some models certificated by the FAA. The heads are liquid-cooled and the cylinders are cooled by ram air. On the 914, the oil is carried in a tank in a dry-sump system, and a camshaft-driven pump forces it through a cooler and filter. Ignition is a dual breakerless capacitor discharge unit, firing order 1-4-2-3, that needs no battery. The 914 also has an exhaust-driven turbocharger, with an electronically controlled wastegate that sets the boost pressure.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 439-442 (the four-cylinder, four-stroke horizontally opposed engine with liquid-cooled heads and ram-air-cooled cylinders; low weight-to-power ratio, narrow silhouette, low vibration; same weight as the Rotax 582; ASTM approved with some models FAA-certificated; the Rotax 914 cooling circuit with expansion tank and overflow bottle; its dry-sump lubrication with oil tank, cooler and camshaft-driven pump; the dual breakerless capacitor discharge ignition with integrated generator, needing no external power, firing order 1-4-2-3; the exhaust gas turbocharger and electronically controlled wastegate). The handbook says its light-sport maintenance notes are for education and not for actual maintenance: the current manufacturer's instructions always apply. The course deck (slide 272) calls the Rotax 912 air and liquid cooled, opposed, and the most common in light-sport aircraft; the handbook text read here describes the 914.

mediaPlan.rationale: Description of one widely used engine; the 3D course engine is a larger relative.

steps.title: Jabiru and other engines
steps.prompt: The Jabiru 2200 is a four-cylinder, four-stroke, horizontally opposed, air-cooled engine of 2,200 cc that gives 85 hp at 3,300 rpm and weighs 132 lb installed, with ram-air ducts in place of baffles and direct propeller drive. The Jabiru 3300 is a six-cylinder 120 hp version. Both have fixed ignition timing, dual magneto-type ignition and hydraulic lifters. Others appear too: Volkswagen conversions, and the Continental O-200, a four-cylinder, carbureted 100 hp engine at 2,750 rpm that has become popular in light-sport aircraft. Lycoming makes an experimental, non-certificated version of its 233 series for light-sport aircraft.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 443-448 (the Jabiru 2200 cc: four-cylinder, four-stroke, horizontally opposed, air-cooled, 85 hp at 3,300 rpm, 132 lb, two ram-air cooling ducts in place of baffles and plenum, direct drive, firing order 1-3-2-4, 25 degrees BTDC; the Jabiru 3300: six-cylinder, 120 hp at 3,300 rpm, 178 lb, firing order 1-4-5-2-3-6, fixed timing; hydraulic lifters; Volkswagen conversions; the Teledyne Continental O-200, four-cylinder carbureted, 100 bhp at 2,750 rpm, 201 cu in, popular for light-sport aircraft; the Lycoming O-233, an experimental non-certificated version). The course deck (slides 271 and 272) also lists the Hirth F23 two-stroke and the ULPower UL260i, which the handbook text read here does not mention.

mediaPlan.rationale: A set of engines to recognise; the matching check tests a few of them.

steps.title: Engines side by side
steps.prompt:
Compare the engines on what the sources give.

Jabiru 2200: four-stroke flat four, air-cooled, direct drive, 85 hp at 3,300 rpm, 132 lb installed.

Jabiru 3300: four-stroke flat six, air-cooled, direct drive, 120 hp at 3,300 rpm, 178 lb.

HKS 700T: four-stroke flat twin, turbocharged and intercooled, geared 2.13 to 1, 80 hp at 5,300 rpm, 126 lb.

Rotax 914: four-stroke flat four, liquid-cooled heads, turbocharged, dry sump.

Rotax 582: two-stroke twin, liquid-cooled, with a gearbox and shock absorber.

Power for each pound: 0.64 hp/lb (Jabiru 2200), 0.67 (Jabiru 3300) and 0.63 (HKS 700T). The GTSIO-520-H gives 375 ÷ 550 = 0.68. Different engines, much the same ratio. What differs is the rpm, the gearing, the cooling and the cycle.
steps.note: Data from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 436 to 445 (the Rotax two-stroke and four-stroke engines, including the 914's liquid-cooled heads, dry sump and turbocharger; the Jabiru 2200 (85 hp at 3,300 rpm, 132 lb) and 3300 (120 hp at 3,300 rpm, 178 lb); the HKS 700T (80 hp takeoff at 5,300 rpm, 126 lb total engine weight)) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152 to 153 (375 hp; dry weight 550.39 lb). The weights are as the handbook gives them (installed for the Jabiru, total engine for the HKS) and are not strictly comparable; the hp-per-pound figures are the lesson's quotients. No weight or output is given in the pages read for the Rotax engines.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The category sets the rules
steps.prompt:
A certificate of airworthiness states the category the aircraft may be flown in: commercial air transport (passenger), commercial air transport (cargo), general aviation or aerial work. The aircraft may be flown only for that kind of purpose.

Some aircraft do not qualify for a certificate of airworthiness. For them the regulations allow a restricted certificate: microlight, experimental amateur-built and kit-built aircraft, aircraft used for air races or exhibitions, and kites. The Authority issues specific operating limitations for each one, and the aircraft may not make international flights.

So the category and the certificate of an aircraft decide what it may do, and with that, which maintenance programme and limits apply to it.

The first thing to learn about a light aircraft is which certificate it holds and what limitations are written on it.
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, regulation 9(4) and (5) (the categories of a certificate of airworthiness: commercial air transport (passenger), commercial air transport (cargo), general aviation, aerial work; the purposes for which the aircraft may be flown), regulation 16 (restricted certificate of airworthiness for aircraft that do not qualify for a certificate of airworthiness, including microlight, experimental amateur and kit built aircraft, air races, exhibition and kites; subject to operating limitations within the United Republic and not to make international flights; the Authority shall issue specific operating limitations for each restricted certificate) and regulation 17 (special flight permits), revised edition 2026, read from the TCAA website on 13 October 2026. The statement that the category decides which maintenance programme and limits apply is the lesson's inference from these.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Who may work on an aircraft in Tanzania
steps.prompt:
The Tanzanian airworthiness regulations list who may maintain an aircraft: a licensed aircraft maintenance engineer, a person working under that engineer's supervision, an approved maintenance organisation, and a pilot licensed by the Authority.

The pilot may do preventive maintenance only, and only on an aircraft of 5,700 kg or less that the pilot owns or operates, that is not used by an air operator, and when the pilot has attended a maintenance course on the type. Preventive maintenance is a short list, which includes replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap.

An engineer may sign only for what is entered on the licence, only when familiar with the airworthiness information for the aircraft, and only with six months of recent experience in the last 24.

Work not done by an organisation needs a maintenance release signed by a properly licensed person.
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, revised edition 2026, regulation 26(2) to (5) (the persons authorised to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance and modification: a licensed pilot, a person under the supervision of a licensed aircraft maintenance engineer, a LAME, an AMO; a pilot may perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft of maximum certificated take-off mass of 5,700 kg or less owned or operated by that pilot, not listed for use by an AOC holder, when the pilot has attended a maintenance course on the type) and regulation 29(t) (replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting of spark plug gap clearance); the Civil Aviation (Personnel Licensing) Regulations, revised edition 2026, regulations 127 and 128 (privileges exercised only for what is entered on the licence, with familiarity with the relevant information and at least six months' experience within the preceding 24 months); and the Civil Aviation (Operation of Aircraft - General Aviation) Regulations, 2024, regulations 36 and 39 (maintenance by an approved maintenance organisation or by a qualified person under authorised procedures with a maintenance release signed by a person licensed under the Personnel Licensing Regulations). All read from the TCAA website on 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: How another state does it
steps.prompt:
Other states set the privileges differently, and the FAA handbook shows the US way as an example.

In the United States the holder of a powerplant certificate can maintain and inspect light-sport engines. A sport pilot may do preventive maintenance on a light-sport aircraft that the pilot owns or operates. A light-sport repairman can hold two ratings. With an inspection rating, which needs a 16-hour course, the holder may do the annual condition inspection on an experimental light-sport aircraft that they own. With a maintenance rating, which needs at least 120 hours of training for airplanes, the holder may approve for return to service after maintenance, the annual condition inspection and the 100-hour inspection of an aircraft with a special airworthiness certificate.

The pattern is the same as in Tanzania: privileges follow the certificate and the person's authorisation.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 435-436 (a powerplant certificate holder can perform maintenance and inspection; a sport pilot may perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft the pilot owns or operates with a special light-sport airworthiness certificate; the repairman certificate (light-sport aircraft) with an inspection rating, a 16-hour course, annual condition inspection of an owned experimental aircraft; with a maintenance rating, training of 120 hours for airplanes; return to service after maintenance, the annual condition inspection and the 100-hour inspection under 14 CFR 91.327). This is the US framework, kept as an example of how another state arranges the same ideas; it does not apply in Tanzania. The course deck (slides 269 and 270) gives the same roles and adds the EASA side (B1.2 or B3 licence holders), which the handbook does not cover and the instructor should confirm.

mediaPlan.rationale: Roles and privileges as a list; a matching check tests them.

steps.title: Find the rules first
steps.prompt:
Before you touch the engine of a light aircraft, find out five things.

Where is it registered, and what does that State's authority require?

What certificate does it hold, in what category, and what limitations are written on it?

Whose data applies? The current manufacturer's instructions, and any mandatory airworthiness directives and service bulletins, which must be complied with.

What does your own licence let you sign for, and are you current?

Is the job preventive maintenance, a repair or an overhaul, and who must inspect and sign it?

If you cannot answer one of them, stop and ask. Work done without the right privilege is unauthorised work, and it can leave an aircraft that looks airworthy and is not.
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, regulation 15 (a person shall not operate an aircraft to which an airworthiness directive applies except in accordance with it; mandatory service bulletins apply; the Authority may prescribe inspections, procedures and limitations for mandatory compliance), regulation 16, regulation 26 and regulation 30 (the manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness) and the Personnel Licensing Regulations, regulation 127 (privileges). The five questions are the lesson's way of putting the instructor's outcome 8 (an engineer must determine the applicable regulatory framework and maintenance privileges before carrying out maintenance).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Daily and preflight checks
steps.prompt: Maintenance on these engines begins with a safe habit: the ignition is off, and the ignition system is grounded. As long as the ground lead is not properly connected, the ignition is live, even if the switch says off. For a Rotax engine the preflight list includes: ignition off, fuel content, coolant leaks, oil tank content, spark plug connectors, oil leaks from the engine and gearbox, loose or missing fasteners, propeller condition and mounting, free and full movement of the throttle, oil pump and choke, the cooling fan turning, and the exhaust. Repair every discrepancy before flight. Rotating the engine by hand to listen for noises is done only after double-checking the ignition off.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 449 (ignition off and grounded, battery disconnected; as long as the ground cable (P-lead) is not properly connected to ground, the ignition is switched on, hot) and PDF pp. 454-455 (the Rotax preflight checklist: verify ignition off, fuel content, coolant leaks, oil tank content, spark plug connectors, oil leaks, loose or missing nuts and bolts, propeller splits and mounting, free and full actuation of throttle, oil pump and choke, cooling fan turns, exhaust; repair all discrepancies before flight; rotate the engine by hand and listen for unusual noises after double verifying ignition off), the same list on EASA Module 16, PDF p. 356. The course deck (slide 273) adds the 50-hour and 100-hour or annual checks.

mediaPlan.rationale: The safety rule about the ground lead is the most important point of the step.

steps.title: Leak-down on a light-sport engine
steps.prompt: The handbook's Jabiru notes give two ways to check compression. A compression gauge reading below 6 bar (90 psi), taken at full throttle with the oil at 30 to 70°C, means the pistons, cylinders, valves and heads need checking. The better test is the pressure differential, or leak-down, test: set the input to 80 psi with the piston at top dead centre on the firing stroke and the propeller restrained. A reading of lower than 80/60, a loss of about 25 percent, shows a problem. Blow-by through the crankcase vent means worn rings or bore. Leaking from the carburettor means a poor intake valve seal, from the exhaust a poor exhaust valve seal, and at the head a poor head-to-cylinder seal.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 457 (in the Jabiru maintenance notes: the compression gauge method, with readings below 6 bar (90 psi) at full throttle and oil temperature 30 to 70 degrees C needing a check of pistons, cylinders, valves and heads; the pressure differential test, a maximum allowable loss of 25 percent, input pressure best set at 80 psi, piston at top dead centre on the firing stroke, the propeller restrained, lower than 80/60 indicating a problem; blow-by through the crankcase vent indicates worn rings or bore, leaking from the carburetor a poor intake valve seal, from the exhaust a poor exhaust valve seal, a head leak a poor head-to-cylinder seal). The handbook says its light-sport maintenance notes are for education and not for actual maintenance: the current manufacturer's instructions always apply.

mediaPlan.rationale: The same test the learner met in the Maintenance & Servicing lesson, with the light-sport limit.

steps.title: What a plug and a chip tell you
steps.prompt: Two small parts reveal the engine's health. Take the plugs out of a warm engine and look at the tip. Light brown means the plug is working correctly. A black, velvety, sooty tip generally means a mixture that is too rich, so check the choke, the air filter and the intake. A tip covered in oil means too much oil in the combustion chamber, so check for worn piston rings and cylinder walls. The Rotax magnetic plug collects metal from the gearbox and engine. A significant amount of chips means the engine must be inspected, repaired or overhauled, and a few steel chips under about 3 mm can be tolerated, but an unclear finding calls for flushing the oil circuit and a new filter.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 457 (in the Jabiru maintenance notes: with plugs removed from a warm engine, a light brown tip means the plug is operating correctly, a black velvet sooty tip generally an overly rich mixture, a tip covered in oil too much oil in the combustion chamber, to check for worn piston rings and cylinder walls; do not use steel or brass brushes and never sandblast plugs) and PDF p. 454 (in the Rotax notes: the magnetic plug is inspected for accumulation of chips, which shows the internal condition of the gearbox and engine; a significant amount of metal chips means the engine must be inspected, repaired or overhauled; steel chips in low numbers can be tolerated if the accumulation is below 3 mm; unclear findings call for flushing the oil circuit, a new oil filter, a test run and another inspection). The course deck (slide 275) asks plug-tip diagnosis as a recap question.

mediaPlan.rationale: Two small parts that give the technician information; a matching check covers the plug tips.

steps.title: When something goes wrong
steps.prompt: Troubleshoot in an organised way: for fuel, start at the tank, then the fittings, the filter and the float chamber; for spark, check each plug. Leave complex problems to an engine technician. Knocking under load can mean fuel of too low an octane rating, or fuel starvation and a lean mixture. An engine that keeps running with the ignition off is overheated, and should be left to cool at about 2,000 rpm idle. Exceeding the maximum engine speed means reducing speed. Exceeding the cylinder head or exhaust gas temperature limit means reducing power to the minimum necessary and making a precautionary landing. In every case the pilot enters the overage in the logbook, with its duration and extent.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 455-456 (in the Rotax notes: organised troubleshooting, fuel first (tank, fittings, filter, float chamber) and spark; engine keeps running with ignition off from overheating, let it cool at about 2,000 rpm; knocking under load from too low an octane rating, or fuel starvation and a lean mixture; exceeding maximum engine speed, cylinder head or exhaust gas temperature: reduce speed or power, make a precautionary landing and enter the overage in the logbook with duration and extent), the same on EASA Module 16, PDF p. 357. The course deck (slide 274) lists symptoms and likely causes in a table of its own (rough idle, hot running, power loss on climb, high fuel consumption, vibration), which the handbook does not give and the instructor should confirm. The handbook says its light-sport maintenance notes are for education and not for actual maintenance: the current manufacturer's instructions always apply.

mediaPlan.rationale: Symptoms and first actions the learner will use in the practical sessions.

steps.title: Plan an inspection
steps.prompt:
A customer brings in a two-seat light aircraft with a four-cylinder opposed engine. The engine is rough at idle and runs hot in the climb. The owner is a licensed pilot and asks what they may do themselves.

Say in your own words what you would find out about the aircraft's certificate and the rules before you start. Then say what you would check first, in what order, and why; which test you would use to judge the cylinders and what reading would worry you; what the plug tips and the magnetic plug could tell you; and which of the work the owner could do as preventive maintenance, and which must be done and signed by a licensed engineer or an approved organisation.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the lesson (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 434-458, with the course deck (slide 274, rough engine at idle and an engine that runs hot among its symptoms). The learner works with the handbook's limits for the engines described and is reminded that the current manufacturer's instructions apply.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner plans the job in their own words.

lessons.title: Practicals
lessons.objective: Prepare for the three practical sessions: follow the observe, name, describe method, work safely around an engine and its propeller, name the main internal and external parts of a reciprocating engine and the items where it meets the aircraft, and inspect the outside of an engine in a fixed order.
lessons.purpose: Demonstrate whether the conceptual knowledge from Lessons 1–17 can actually be recognised and applied physically.

outcomes.heading: Practical A — Demonstration of Piston-Engine Operation
items: Identify TDC and BDC.
Demonstrate intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes.
Relate piston movement to crankshaft rotation.
Explain crankshaft-to-camshaft speed relationship.
Observe and explain valve opening and closing.
Demonstrate valve timing.
Identify lead, lag and overlap where visible on the trainer.
Explain the sequence of energy conversion from combustion pressure to crankshaft rotation.
Explain how firing events in multiple cylinders combine to produce smoother engine rotation.
Explain the complete operation of a four-stroke reciprocating engine while manipulating or observing the training engine.

outcomes.heading: Practical B — External & Internal Component Identification and Condition
outcomes.note: The emphasis: identify it → state its function → describe its construction → recognise abnormal condition.
items: Identify principal externally visible engine components.
State the function of each identified component.
Identify the crankcase, accessory case and sump.
Identify engine mounts and shock mounts.
Locate induction, exhaust, ignition, lubrication and accessory interfaces.
Identify representative internal components from dismantled or sectioned assemblies.
Identify pistons, rings, piston pins, connecting rods, crankshaft, bearings, cylinders and valves.
Identify representative valve-train components.
Distinguish major materials and construction features where visible.
Recognise obvious leakage, corrosion, cracks, wear, scoring, overheating, deposits and physical damage.
Relate an observed defect to the likely function of the affected component.

outcomes.heading: Practical C — Engine Maintenance Procedures
items: Safely dismantle/disassemble a selected piston-engine power-generation assembly.
Identify components as they are removed.
Inspect representative components for obvious condition and serviceability.
Reassemble the selected power-generation assembly in the correct relationship.
Demonstrate or perform appropriate hydraulic-tappet servicing.
Inspect valve-train components for corrosion and wear.
Perform or demonstrate a valve-spring compression check using appropriate training equipment.
Inspect representative exhaust-system components.
Identify cracks, leakage, deterioration and attachment problems in an exhaust system.
Demonstrate appropriate periodic exhaust-system maintenance/inspection.
Follow appropriate workshop practices, tools and maintenance information while performing practical tasks.

lessons.syllabusNote: The module itself states that workshop practices should be used to develop understanding and specifically identifies engine parts and a piston-engine trainer among the intended learning materials; the lesson is formalised as three practical exercises. They are particularly important because the official module does not stop at theoretical understanding: it explicitly requires students to dismantle and reassemble power-generation assemblies, service hydraulic tappets, inspect valve-train components and check valve-spring compression. It also requires periodic exhaust-system maintenance.
lessons.completionCriteria: Say which working area and which practical each session belongs to; explain the four strokes, TDC and BDC, the camshaft's half speed, valve lead, lag and overlap, and how firing events in several cylinders smooth the turning; identify and describe the main internal and external parts, their materials and the signs of a defect, and relate a defect to what the part does; describe in order how a cylinder is taken off and put back, how a hydraulic tappet is serviced and tested, how a valve and its spring are checked and how an exhaust system is inspected at intervals; and say why the manufacturer's manual, the right tools and the regulations come first.

steps.title: Four sessions, three practicals
steps.prompt:
You will work in four places, on real engines.

Session I, in the HighTech Powerplant Lab: the cut-away O-360, with its mechanism moving. This is Practical A.

Session II, in the Hangar: two disassembled engines, one with a four-throw crankshaft and one with six. You name and describe their parts.

Session III, in the Aviation Complex Powerplant Room and the Hangar: the assembled GTSIO-520 engines and the assembled O-360, seen from outside.

Session IV, outside the Hangar: the engine mounted in the Cessna 182.

Sessions II to IV together are Practical B. Practical C is the set of maintenance tasks, and your instructor says where each is done.

This lesson prepares you. It does not do the worksheets for you.
steps.note: Documented from the instructor's list of the four working areas and which practical belongs to each (13 October 2026) and the instructor's teaching notes, which name the four practicals as I motorised engine mechanism, II internal disassembled components, III external assembled components and IV mounted engine on an aircraft; and from the instructor's three outcome lists (Practicals A, B and C, shown at the top of the lesson). The instructor's list does not say where the Practical C tasks are done, so the step leaves that to the instructor, who should confirm it. The external and internal worksheets are the instructor's Practical 1 and Practical 2 documents.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Observe, name, describe
