steps.prompt: Every row of a worksheet asks for the same things. Observe: look at the component from at least two angles, then draw a clear sketch or paste a photograph. Name: write the correct aviation engineering name in full, with no abbreviations. Describe: say what the component does in one or two concise sentences. Record: note its type or variant, its material, where it sits, any dimensions or specifications, and anything that bears on airworthiness, such as security, leakage, corrosion or wear. If you are not sure of a name, ask and look it up in the handbook. Why do you think the worksheet asks for your own words, and not a copied description?
steps.note: Documented from the student practical worksheets: the internal worksheet instructions (examine each numbered component, sketch or photograph it, write the correct aviation engineering name with no abbreviations, state its function in one or two concise sentences, record material, type or variant, relevant dimensions or specifications and airworthiness considerations) and the external worksheet instructions (observe each component from at least two angles; record type, material, location and airworthiness considerations such as security, leakage, corrosion and wear; the student declaration that all entries are the student's own work).

mediaPlan.rationale: The method is the content; the learner practises it in the last step.

steps.title: Safety at the engine
steps.prompt: An engine can hurt you before it ever runs. The FAA handbook gives a warning for moving a propeller. Before you turn it: disconnect all spark plug leads; check that the magneto switches are connected and off, with the P-leads grounded; close the throttle; set the mixture to idle cut-off; set the brakes, block the wheels and fit the tie-downs; and never stand in the arc of the propeller blades. Your worksheets add two rules: do not climb on the aircraft or open inspection panels without your instructor's permission, and stay clear of the propeller arc at all times. Why is a propeller that is only being turned by hand still dangerous?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 347 (the warning, printed in the procedure for taking an engine out of storage: before moving the propeller, disconnect all spark plug leads, verify that the magneto switches are connected and off and the P-leads grounded, throttle closed, mixture idle cut-off, brakes set, wheels blocked, tie-downs installed, cabin door latch open, and do not stand within the arc of the propeller blades; the lesson treats it as the general rule) and the external student worksheet safety notice (no climbing on the aircraft or opening inspection panels without instructor permission; stay clear of the propeller arc). The handbook also says in the light-sport notes, PDF p. 449, that a P-lead that is not grounded leaves the ignition live.

mediaPlan.rationale: The warning is the content; the check asks which actions belong to it.

steps.title: Safety in each working area
steps.prompt:
Each area has its own hazards, and your instructor's briefing comes first.

At the cutaway, the mechanism moves, and the casing is cut away so the moving parts are exposed. Keep hands, hair, sleeves and anything that hangs well clear of every moving part, and leave starting and stopping to your instructor.

At the disassembled engines, parts are heavy and edges are sharp. Lift with care, ask for help with a heavy part, and keep tools and parts off the floor.

Around the Cessna, the propeller rules in the last step apply, and you stay off the aircraft unless you are told.

If you are not sure something is safe, stop and ask. Which hazard here could hurt you even when nothing is running?
steps.note: Written for this lesson from general workshop practice, to go with the instructor's list of the four working areas. It is not taken from a manual or a regulation, and the instructor should replace or confirm it with each area's own rules. The rules for the aircraft are the FAA propeller warning in the previous step and the external worksheet's notice (no climbing on the aircraft or opening inspection panels without the instructor's permission; stay clear of the propeller arc).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: TDC, BDC and the four strokes
steps.prompt:
The piston slides up and down in the cylinder. The top of its travel is top dead centre, TDC. The bottom is bottom dead centre, BDC. The distance between them is the stroke.

The four strokes are intake, compression, power and exhaust. They take two complete turns of the crankshaft, 720 degrees, so each cylinder fires once in every two turns.

In this model the piston is at BDC, where the intake stroke ends and compression begins.

At the cutaway, find the piston at the top and at the bottom of its travel. Say which strokes carry the piston up and which carry it down. Then say where the piston is at the end of the compression stroke.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 46 (the four-stroke cycle: four strokes to complete the operating cycle of each cylinder; two complete revolutions of the crankshaft, 720 degrees, so each cylinder fires once in every two revolutions; the stroke is the distance the piston moves from TDC to BDC; Figure 1-35, components and terminology) and PDF p. 47 (the intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes, Figure 1-36). The cycle angle of 180 degrees is the bottom of the intake stroke, where compression begins (the model caption names the stroke that follows). The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model shows the piston at one end of its travel so the learner can name the position before watching it move on the cutaway.

steps.title: The camshaft turns at half speed
steps.prompt:
A cycle takes two turns of the crankshaft, and each valve opens only once in a cycle. So the camshaft turns once while the crankshaft turns twice. It runs at half the crankshaft speed.

In an opposed engine a gear on the camshaft meshes with a gear on the crankshaft. The camshaft gear is twice the size, which gives the ratio of 2 to 1.

At the cutaway, find the crankshaft, the camshaft and the gears that join them. Watch both for a few turns: the crankshaft should turn twice for each turn of the camshaft. As the cam lobe passes under its tappet, watch which valve opens.

Which gear has more teeth, the camshaft gear or the crankshaft gear?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 41 (the valve mechanism of an opposed engine is operated by a camshaft driven by a gear that mates with another gear attached to the crankshaft; the camshaft always rotates at one-half the crankshaft speed; Figure 1-28: the cam gear is twice the size of the crankshaft gear and operates at half speed) and the Valve Operating lesson. The handbook describes opposed engines in general; the lesson does not state how the cut-away O-360 is built, and the instructor should confirm that its gears are as the handbook describes.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Lead, lag and overlap
steps.prompt:
The camshaft opens each valve early and closes it late.

The intake valve opens before TDC, while the exhaust stroke is still finishing: that is valve lead. The exhaust valve closes after TDC, once the intake stroke has begun: that is valve lag. For a short time both valves are off their seats. That is valve overlap. It helps to cool the cylinder from inside, to draw in more charge and to clear out the burned gas.

Find the overlap on the handbook's chart. The angles are in degrees of crankshaft travel, and each marks where a valve starts to open, not where it is fully open.

On the cutaway, look for the moment near TDC when both valves are open, if you can see it.
steps.alt: Valve timing chart drawn as a spiral of coloured dots for one complete four-stroke cycle: intake in orange starting 50 degrees before top centre where the intake valve opens, compression in green with ignition just before top centre, power in red with the exhaust valve opening 30 degrees before bottom centre, and exhaust in blue ending 25 degrees after top centre where the exhaust valve closes; a blue arc across the top marks the 75 degree valve overlap with both valves open.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 39 (valve overlap: both valves open at the end of the exhaust stroke and the beginning of the intake stroke; better volumetric efficiency and lower cylinder operating temperature) and PDF p. 47 (the intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke, valve lead; the exhaust valve closes well after TDC, valve lag; the overlap helps to cool the cylinder internally, to increase the charge and to scavenge the byproducts of combustion; the timing is in degrees of crankshaft travel and marks the start of opening; Figure 1-37). The chart's angles are the handbook's example, not the cut-away engine's: the cylinder model in this course uses illustrative ideal timing with no overlap, so only the real engine or the manufacturer's data gives its timing.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook chart is a real timing diagram; the learner finds the overlap on it before looking for the moment on the engine.

steps.title: From pressure to crankshaft
steps.prompt:
Energy changes form in a fixed order. Burning mixture raises the pressure in the cylinder. The pressure pushes the piston down. The piston pushes on the connecting rod through the piston pin. The rod pushes on the crankpin, which sits off the centre line of the crankshaft, so the push becomes a turning effort. The crankshaft turns the propeller. Heat energy has become mechanical energy.

In this model the piston is a short way past TDC on the power stroke.

At the cutaway, follow the path from the piston to the crankshaft and name each part in turn. Which part changes the up-and-down motion into rotation?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 46 (an internal combustion engine converts heat energy into mechanical energy; the downward motion of the piston, acting on the crankshaft through the connecting rod, is converted to rotary motion by the crankshaft) and PDF p. 29 (the crankpin is off-center from the main journals and is called the throw; a force on the crankpin that is not through the centre line causes the crankshaft to rotate). The sequence is the same as in the Power Generation lesson. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model isolates the piston, pin, rod and crank throw just after TDC on the power stroke, so the path of the force can be named.

steps.title: Many cylinders, smoother turning
steps.prompt:
One cylinder pushes on the crankshaft only once in two turns. The momentum of the crankshaft and propeller carries it through the other strokes. More cylinders fill the gaps.

A four-cylinder engine such as the O-360 fires one cylinder every 720 ÷ 4 = 180 degrees of crankshaft turn. The six-cylinder GTSIO-520 fires every 720 ÷ 6 = 120 degrees. A power stroke lasts 180 degrees, so on the six-cylinder engine the next cylinder fires while the last is still pushing, and the turning is smoother.

The firing order is chosen for balance, and it is not simply 1, 2, 3, 4.

Watch the cutaway through two turns of the crankshaft. How many power strokes do you expect to count?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 46 (the momentum of the crankshaft and the propeller forces the piston back up; two revolutions, 720 degrees, for the four strokes) and PDF p. 37 (the firing order is the sequence in which the power event occurs in the different cylinders, designed for balance and to eliminate vibration; one four-cylinder opposed model fires 1-4-2-3 and another 1-3-2-4). The intervals 720 divided by the number of cylinders, and the 180-degree length of a stroke, are the lesson's arithmetic, as in the Power Generation lesson. The lesson does not state the cut-away O-360's firing order, because the handbook says it differs between models.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Explain it at the cutaway
steps.prompt:
The outcome for this practical is that you can explain the complete operation of a four-stroke engine while you watch or handle the training engine.

Prepare for it. Choose one cylinder. For each of the four strokes say, in order, where the piston is and which way it moves; whether each valve is open or shut; what is happening to the gas; and what the crankshaft and the camshaft are doing.

Then say how the cylinders together keep the crankshaft turning, and how the chemical energy of the fuel ends up as the turning of the propeller.

If you cannot say one stroke, go back to its step. Which stroke do you find hardest to put into words?
steps.note: Documented from the instructor's Practical A outcomes (explain the complete operation of a four-stroke reciprocating engine while manipulating or observing the training engine; explain the sequence of energy conversion; explain how firing events in multiple cylinders combine to produce smoother rotation). The step is a self-explanation prompt: the lesson sets out no model answer beyond the earlier steps, and what the assessor looks for is the instructor's to say.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Session II: count the throws
steps.prompt:
The two disassembled engines in the Hangar Engine Room are in pieces, and every part is within reach. Start by counting.

A crankshaft is made of main journals, crank cheeks and crankpins. A crankpin is also called a throw: it is where a connecting rod fits. The handbook says the number of throws must match the cylinder arrangement, and that a four-throw crankshaft suits a four-cylinder opposed engine, and a six-throw one a six-cylinder opposed engine.

Count the throws on each engine. Then count the pistons and rods laid out beside it. Do the numbers agree? If a part is missing from the set, say so.

Then confirm with your instructor what each engine is.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 29 (the crankshaft has a journal, crankpin and crank cheek; two crank cheeks and a crankpin make a throw; the four-throw construction may be used on four-cylinder horizontal opposed or four-cylinder inline engines, and the six-throw shaft on six-cylinder inline engines, 12-cylinder V-type engines and six-cylinder opposed engines; the number of crankpins must correspond with the cylinder arrangement of the engine) and the instructor's list (one disassembled engine with four crankshaft throws and one with six). The lesson does not say which engines they are; the instructor does.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Name the big parts first
steps.prompt: On the engine in front of you, start with the big parts, because every other part is attached to one of them. Find the crankcase halves, the accessory case at the rear, the oil sump and a cylinder. Name these first, then work out towards the small parts. A part is much easier to name once you know what it sits next to, and what lies on either side of it.
steps.alt: FAA exploded view of an opposed engine showing the crankcase halves, accessory case, oil sump, crankshaft, camshaft, cylinder and accessories
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26-28 (nose section, accessory section, Figure 1-6), as in the Parts and Construction lesson. Sump construction differs by engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA exploded view names every major case section and accessory in one labelled figure.

steps.title: Piston, rings and pin
steps.prompt: Pick up a piston and look for three things. The top, the piston head, takes the pressure of combustion. Below it are the ring grooves: this piston carries four rings, two compression rings above and two oil-control rings below, and a technician names them by position, top ring first. Across the middle is the bore for the piston pin, which joins the piston to the connecting rod. A soft aluminium plug in each end of the pin stops the pin scoring the cylinder wall. Count the grooves, then name each ring.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 33-35 (the piston pin must be held in place to prevent its ends scoring the cylinder walls, and a plug of relatively soft aluminum in the pin end gives a bearing surface against the wall, PDF p. 34), and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1g (PDF p. 17): aluminium alloy pistons, a four-ring piston since 1975, and full-floating ground steel pins with forged-in aluminium plugs. Ring names follow the component labels of the reviewed cylinder model. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model isolates the piston, its four rings and the pin so each can be named.

steps.title: Rod, bearing and crankshaft
steps.prompt: The connecting rod joins the piston to the crankshaft. At one end, the small end carries a bushing around the piston pin. Along the middle, the shank is shaped like an I-beam, strong but light. At the other end, the big end is split so it can be put together around the crankpin: the cap is held on by two bolts with slotted nuts, and bearing halves sit between the rod and the crankshaft. The crankshaft throw is the offset part that the big end wraps round. Name each of these in order, from piston to crankshaft.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 29-32, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraphs 3-1e and 3-1f (PDF pp. 16-17): I-beam rods and two precision inserts at the crankpin end. Part names follow the component labels of the reviewed cylinder model, which shows one crankshaft throw. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model isolates the rod, its bearing halves, bolts and the crankshaft throw.

steps.title: Valves and rocker arms
steps.prompt: Each cylinder has two valves in its head: one lets the fresh charge in, and the other lets the burned gas out. On a real engine you can often tell them apart by what is connected to their ports: the induction system on the intake side, and the exhaust stack on the other. Each valve is pressed shut by springs and is opened by a rocker arm, which is moved by a pushrod from the camshaft. Find both valves and both rocker arms. Which valve do you expect to run hotter, and why?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 38-42 (valves, springs, rocker arms, pushrods and the cam follower; PDF p. 38: intake valves operate at lower temperatures than exhaust valves, so exhaust valves are made of more heat-resistant alloys) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 16, as in the Valve Operating lesson. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model isolates both valves and both rocker arms in the head.

steps.title: Valve-train parts in order
steps.prompt:
Lay the valve-train parts out in the order the motion passes through them. The cam lobe lifts the tappet, or lifter body. The tappet moves the pushrod, which runs inside its housing. The pushrod tips the rocker arm on its shaft. The rocker arm presses down on the valve stem. The valve spring closes the valve again.

On a disassembled engine, keep the pushrods in order and mark them: the ball ends wear to fit their sockets, and the rods are not always the same length.

Find each part on the model and then on the engine. Which part do the springs push against at the top?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 38 to 42 (the valve-operating mechanism: cam, cam follower, push rod, rocker arm, valve, the springs held by the retaining washer and stem keys; the push rod's hardened-steel ball ends) and PDF p. 410 (mark the push rods so they are replaced in the same location; the ball ends are worn to fit their sockets; push rods are not all of the same length on some engines). The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exploded stage of the cylinder model separates the lifter, pushrod, rocker arm and valve so the order can be named.

steps.title: Materials and construction
steps.prompt:
Where a part is visible, its material tells you something about its job.

A cylinder head is aluminium alloy: a good conductor of heat, and light. It is joined to a steel barrel, and the cooling fins are machined as part of the barrel.

Most pistons are machined from aluminium alloy forgings. Piston rings are most often gray cast iron, and chrome rings must be used with steel cylinder walls, never chrome ones.

A crankshaft is forged from strong alloy steel, and the bearing surfaces are hardened by nitriding.

A crankcase is cast aluminium alloy, and sometimes magnesium.

An exhaust valve is made of a heat-resistant alloy, because it runs hotter than an intake valve.

Find one example of each, and say which parts you cannot check without taking them apart.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023): PDF p. 26 (cast or forged aluminum alloy generally used for crankcases because it is light and strong), PDF p. 27 and p. 28 (crankcase sections of aluminum alloy or magnesium), PDF p. 29 (crankshafts forged from a very strong alloy such as chromium-nickel-molybdenum steel; the crankpin outer surface hardened by nitriding), PDF pp. 33 and 34 (pistons machined from aluminum alloy forgings; gray cast iron most often used for piston rings; chrome rings must be used with steel cylinder walls), PDF pp. 35 and 36 (aluminum alloy cylinder head, a good conductor of heat and light; steel barrel; cooling fins machined as an integral part of the barrel) and PDF p. 38 (exhaust valves made of heat-resistant alloys because intake valves operate at lower temperatures).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Session III: what is fitted at the rear
steps.prompt: The accessory section at the rear is where gears turned by the crankshaft drive the parts that keep the engine going: two magnetos for ignition, an engine-driven fuel pump, an oil pump and a tachometer drive, and a starter and an alternator. Where each one sits depends on the engine, and this teaching model moves some of them onto display stands, so always check the engine in front of you. Name each accessory, and say which one turns the engine instead of being turned by it.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28 (accessory case, mounting pads and geared shafts) and PDF p. 236 (the starter clutch), and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, A-3-2 and Figure A-4-8 (PDF pp. 17 and 25), with the -H difference data in C-3-2 and C-3-3 (PDF pp. 152-153) and C-3-6 (PDF p. 156), as in the Accessories and Drives lesson, where starting reverses the flow of power. The accessory model is a teaching reconstruction; its scope note says the front and optional modules are relocated on display stands and omitted transfers are not physical shafts.

mediaPlan.rationale: The accessory model shows the magnetos, pump, oil and tachometer drive, starter and alternator in their gear train.

steps.title: Read the engine's name
steps.prompt:
Every engine is named by its features. An opposed engine is named with the letter O and its displacement in cubic inches. Prefixes add features: I for fuel injection, T or TS for a turbo-supercharging system, G for a geared engine, and L for left-hand rotation.

So the O-360 in the Hangar is an opposed engine of 360 cubic inches, with none of the other letters. The GTSIO-520 in the Powerplant Room is geared, turbo-supercharged, fuel-injected and opposed, of 520 cubic inches.

Read the name from the engine's plate, or ask your instructor, before you touch anything. Then see whether what you can see agrees with it: is there a turbocharger, an injection system, a reduction gear at the front?
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16 (core text), PDF p. 6 (opposed engines are designated with the letter O and the piston displacement; the prefix I is fuel injected, T or TS a turbo-supercharging system, G a geared engine; an O-360 is an opposed engine of 360 cubic inches) and the Classification lesson, which reads GTSIO-520 letter by letter. The reading that the O-360 has none of the other letters follows from the key, not from a manual for the Hangar engine. The location of an engine's plate is not stated in the handbook; the instructor can say where to look on each engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Outside parts, system by system
steps.prompt: The external worksheet groups what you can see by system, and it helps to walk the engine in the same order. Cylinders and cooling: the cylinder, its cooling fins and the rocker covers. Ignition: the two magnetos and the harness that carries the spark to each plug. Fuel and induction: the carburettor or fuel-injection servo, the induction manifold and the engine-driven fuel pump. Exhaust: the manifold or stacks. Lubrication: the sump, the oil filter, and the oil cooler and its connections. Accessory drive and power take-off: the propeller flange and the accessory case at the rear. Take one system at a time so nothing is missed.
steps.note: Documented from the external student worksheet, Part A (the component groups: cylinder and cooling, ignition system, fuel and induction, exhaust system, lubrication, accessory drive and power take-off). The lesson names the groups and the parts only; it gives no worksheet answers. The course deck (slide 279) also lists the propeller, starter motor and alternator as external parts, which the worksheet does not list.

mediaPlan.rationale: The groups are a checklist for the walk-round, tested in a matching check.

steps.title: Session IV: engine meets aircraft
steps.prompt: On the aircraft the question changes. You are no longer asking only what a part is, but how the airframe holds the engine and protects the aircraft from it. The engine mount holds the engine to the airframe, often through shock mounts that absorb vibration. The firewall is the foremost bulkhead of the engine compartment, made of stainless steel or another fire-resistant material, so that an engine fire is confined to the nacelle. It is also where the lines, linkages and wiring between engine and aircraft are disconnected. For each part you find, ask: what does it connect, and what happens if it fails?
steps.alt: Photograph of an engine mounting ring on a light aircraft firewall with four dynamic mount fittings
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 27 and 343-344 (mounting lugs, mount ring, dynafocal and shock mounts), EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 275-276 (relative motion between engine and airframe), and FAA PDF pp. 330-331 (the firewall: usually the foremost bulkhead of the engine nacelle, of stainless steel or other fire-resistant material, its primary purpose to confine any engine fire to the nacelle, a mounting surface for units, and a point of disconnect for lines, linkages and wiring). The external worksheet lists the engine mount and the firewall as aircraft-installed items.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook photograph shows a mounting ring and its fittings on a firewall.

steps.title: Bonding, oil access and the heat muff
steps.prompt: Three more items on the aircraft. A bonding strap is an electrical connection between two conducting parts that are not otherwise connected adequately; bonding and grounding give current a return path, protect against lightning and static, and protect people from shock. The oil filler and dipstick access is where the oil is checked and topped up; the dipstick has marks that show the correct level. The exhaust heat muff is a shroud round the exhaust: warm air from around the exhaust can be ducted to the carburettor, and a heat exchanger can warm the cabin. A cracked heat exchanger is a carbon monoxide hazard. Which of these would you check for security, and which for leakage?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 224 (bonding is the electrical connecting of two or more conducting objects not otherwise connected adequately; bonding and grounding protect against lightning, provide current return paths, prevent radio-frequency potentials, protect personnel from shock and prevent static charge), PDF pp. 260 and 277 (oil level checked with the dipstick or a sight gauge, with marks for the correct level), PDF p. 129 (warm ducted air from around the exhaust directed into the carburettor), and PDF pp. 149 and 152 (cabin heater exhaust shroud; failure of heat exchanger surfaces lets exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard, or into the induction system). The external worksheet lists these as aircraft-installed items.

mediaPlan.rationale: Three short items described together; the photograph on the previous step shows the mount and firewall.

steps.title: Notes an inspector can use
steps.prompt: In the notes column, use the words an inspector uses. The handbook defines them. Corrosion is loss of metal by chemical or electrochemical action. Chafing is wear from two parts rubbing together under light pressure. A crack is a partial separation of the material, caused by vibration, overloading, internal stress or fatigue. A dent is a small, rounded depression where the part was struck. Fretting is surface erosion from tiny movements between parts that are clamped together. A good note then says where the damage is, and what it could lead to, for example a chafed hose against a clamp. Pick two parts on the engine and write a note for each in this way.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 371 (the common defect terms and their definitions: chafing, corrosion, crack, dent, fretting, among twenty-six). The worksheets ask for airworthiness considerations such as security, leakage, corrosion and wear in the notes column. The chafed-hose example is the lesson's own illustration, not a handbook case.

mediaPlan.rationale: Definitions tested in a matching check; the learner writes notes in the last step.

steps.title: More words: scoring, burning, pitting
steps.prompt:
Inside the engine, three more words matter.

Scoring is a series of deep scratches, caused by foreign particles between moving parts or by careless assembly or disassembly.

Burning is surface damage from excessive heat. It is usually caused by an improper fit, defective lubrication or over-temperature operation.

Pitting is small hollows of irregular shape, usually caused by corrosion or minute chipping.

Now link the defect to the job. Think of a cylinder wall that is scored, so the rings cannot seal against it. What would you expect the engine to lose? And a valve with a burned face: the handbook says do not reuse it. What could that valve no longer do?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 371 (the defect terms: burning, pitting and scoring, among twenty-six), PDF p. 380 (examine the valve for damage from burning or corrosion; do not re-use valves that indicate damage of this nature) and PDF p. 409 (excessive leakage past the piston is a frequent cause of compression leakage). The links from the defect to what the part does (a scored wall cannot seal, a burned valve face cannot close) are the lesson's own reasoning, drawn from the part's job as the handbook describes it.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: A walk-round in a fixed order
steps.prompt: The visual inspection is a systematic walk-round: always the same order, so nothing is skipped. Cowling and mounts: look for cracks, dents and signs of stress. Hoses and wiring: look for wear, chafing and loose connections. Fluid leaks: oil, fuel or hydraulic. Belts and pulleys: tension and alignment. Cooling fins and air intakes: clean and unobstructed. Exhaust system: corrosion or damage. The handbook adds that scratches, dents and tears in cowl panels weaken them, add drag and start corrosion, and that latches are checked for pulled rivets and loose or damaged handles.
steps.note: Documented from the course deck, slide 280 (the six areas of the visual inspection of external components) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 282 (inspect the cowl panels for scratches, dents and tears, which weaken the panel, increase drag and start corrosion; latches for pulled rivets and loose or damaged handles; the inspections are visual checks performed frequently). The deck refers to an FAA advisory circular on visual inspection without naming it, so it is not cited.

mediaPlan.rationale: The six areas are a list to follow; the next steps show two of them in detail.

steps.title: What the regulations list
steps.prompt:
The Tanzanian airworthiness regulations list what a person performing an inspection must look at on the engine and nacelle. They include: the engine section for excessive oil, fuel or hydraulic leaks, and the source of each; studs and nuts for improper torquing; the engine mount for cracks and looseness, and the engine for looseness on its mount; the flexible vibration dampers for poor condition; engine controls for improper travel and safetying; lines, hoses and clamps for leaks and looseness; exhaust stacks for cracks and improper attachment; accessories for security of mounting; the cowling for cracks.

The inspector works from a checklist. Which of these have you not yet looked for on your walk-round?
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, revised edition 2026, regulation 31(3) (a person who performs an inspection shall use a checklist, which shall include the scope and detail of the items prescribed or approved by the Authority) and regulation 31(6)(c) (the engine and nacelle group: leaks, studs and nuts, internal engine and metal particles on screens and sump drain plugs, engine mount, flexible vibration dampeners, engine controls, lines, hoses and clamps, exhaust stacks, accessories, systems, cowling), read from the TCAA website on 13 October 2026; the TCAA says its published copy is not authoritative. Regulation 31(5) also requires the aircraft and engine to be thoroughly cleaned and the necessary panels, doors and cowlings opened before an inspection; that is the inspection of a complete aircraft, and differs from the handbook's rule to look at disassembled parts before they are cleaned.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Reading an exhaust system
steps.prompt: The exhaust system is one of the first places to look. An exhaust leak shows as a flat gray or sooty black streak on the pipes where the gas escaped, usually at a clamp or an exhaust port joint. Check every external surface for cracks, dents and missing parts, and the welds, clamps, supports, slip joints, flanges, gaskets and flexible couplings. Never mark exhaust parts with a lead pencil, and never use zinc-plated tools on them: the lead or zinc is absorbed when the metal is heated, which softens it and leads to cracks.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of three types of exhaust system, labelled A, B and C, with red arrows marking the primary areas to inspect at joints, flanges, mufflers and heat-exchanger shrouds.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 151 (an exhaust leak is indicated by a flat gray or sooty black streak on the pipes in the area of the leak; close attention to all external surfaces for cracks, dents or missing parts, and to welds, clamps, supports, lugs, bracing, slip joints, flanges, gaskets and flexible couplings; never use galvanized or zinc-plated tools, and never mark exhaust parts with a lead pencil; Figure 3-42, primary inspection areas of three types of exhaust systems).

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook drawing marks the primary inspection areas on three exhaust system layouts.

steps.title: Fins: repair or reject?
steps.prompt: The cooling fins carry heat from the cylinder to the air, so their condition matters. Look for cracks and breaks. The handbook says small cracks are not in themselves a reason to remove a cylinder: they can be filled, or sometimes stop-drilled so they cannot grow, and a sharp corner can be filed smooth. A crack at the base of a fin, however, is a reason to reject the cylinder at overhaul. Too much broken fin leaves a hot spot. On the handbook's example engine, a cylinder is removed if more than 12 inches of one fin is broken off at its base, or more than 83 square inches of fin on one head. Those limits belong to that engine only: for any other, find the manufacturer's.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 282 (the fins are inspected at each regular inspection; small cracks are not a reason for cylinder removal and can be filled or stop-drilled; sharp corners may be filed, after consulting the manufacturer's manual for allowable limits; on a certain engine, more than 12 inches of one fin broken off at its base, or more than 83 square inches of broken fin on one head, means the cylinder is replaced, with limits for adjacent broken fins; the handbook states these specifications apply only to its example engine) and PDF p. 372 (cracks near the edge of the fins are not dangerous if the portion is removed and contoured, cracks at the base of the fin are a reason for rejecting the cylinder).

mediaPlan.rationale: The example limits are in the text with the handbook's own warning that they are engine-specific.

steps.title: Practical C: the maintenance tasks
steps.note: Documented from the instructor's Practical C outcomes (dismantle and reassemble a power-generation assembly; identify components as they are removed; inspect for condition; hydraulic-tappet servicing; valve-train inspection for corrosion and wear; valve-spring compression check; exhaust-system inspection and periodic maintenance; workshop practices, tools and maintenance information) and the module description's statement that students dismantle and reassemble power-generation assemblies, service hydraulic tappets, inspect valve-train components and check valve-spring compression. The instructor's list does not say where these tasks are done, so the step leaves it to the instructor.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Look before you clean
steps.prompt: When parts come off an engine, how you treat them matters. The handbook's practices: lay the parts out in order on a bench, and keep small parts in containers. Drain the oil into a container, strain it through a clean cloth, and check the oil and the cloth for metal particles. Throw away safety wire and cotter pins as they come off, and never use them a second time. Tag any loose or damaged studs and fittings. Use the proper tool for the job, not an improvised one. Above all, look first: a part should not be cleaned before a preliminary visual inspection, because deposits left in recesses may show how it failed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 370-371 (disassembly practices: parts laid out in an orderly manner, containers for small parts, drain and strain the oil through a clean cloth and check for metal particles, dispose of safety devices and never reuse them, tag loose or damaged studs and fittings, use the proper tool; visual inspection should precede all other inspection, and parts should not be cleaned before a preliminary visual inspection). The disassembled-engine session is supervised; the lesson does not describe a procedure to follow without the instructor.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short list of habits from the overhaul chapter.

steps.title: Taking a cylinder off
steps.prompt:
A power assembly is a cylinder with its piston and rod. The handbook gives a general order for taking one off; the manufacturer's manual has the torque values and special precautions for your engine.

Protect every opening so that nuts, washers and tools cannot fall in. Take off the intake and exhaust pipes and the rocker covers. Loosen the spark plugs but leave them in until you are ready to pull the cylinder.

Turn the crankshaft to TDC on the compression stroke, so both rocker arms are free, then take out the pushrods and mark them. Remove all the hold-down nuts but two opposite each other. Support the cylinder, remove those two, and draw it off straight, with a partner. Catch any broken ring pieces with a shop cloth, and support the connecting rod.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 409 and 410 (cylinder removal: the instructions are very general and the applicable manufacturer's manual should be consulted for torque values and special precautions; protect openings so that nuts, washers and tools do not enter the engine; remove the intake and exhaust pipes, loosen the spark plugs and do not remove them until ready to pull the cylinder off; turn the crankshaft to TDC on the compression stroke before removing the push rods, which relieves the pressure on both rocker arms; mark the push rods; remove all but two nuts 180 degrees apart; two technicians working together; a cloth to stop pieces of broken rings falling into the crankcase; support the connecting rod). The step is a description of ideas, not a procedure to follow without the instructor.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Putting a cylinder back
steps.prompt:
Reassembly puts every part back where it came from, the right way round.

Clean the piston and cylinder and check them. Fit the piston to the rod with the number stamped on the piston head toward the front of the engine, and lubricate the pin. Oil the piston and rings well, stagger the ring gaps around the piston, and check that each ring is in its own groove and the right way up. Check that only one cylinder oil-seal ring is in place.

With the piston at TDC, compress the rings with a ring compressor and ease the cylinder on straight and even, without rocking. Fit two nuts opposite each other, then the rest, and torque them slowly and steadily to the value in the manual. Then safety them. Push rods go back in their own places, not turned end for end.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 410 and 411 (cylinder installation: the piston number stamped on the bottom of the piston head faces the front of the engine; lubricate the pin; oil the piston and rings; stagger the ring gaps and check the rings are in the correct grooves and positioned correctly; only one cylinder oil-seal ring; with the piston at TDC, use a ring compressor, and do not rock the cylinder; two nuts 180 degrees apart, then the remaining nuts snug; torque to the value in the manufacturer's manual with a slow, steady motion; safety them; push rods installed in their original locations and not turned end to end; the ball end seated in the tappet; valve clearance set). The step is a description of ideas, not a procedure to follow without the instructor.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Hydraulic tappets: keep the set together
steps.prompt:
A hydraulic tappet holds the valve clearance at zero. Servicing one is clean, careful bench work.

Use a clean bench and unused solvent. Keep the parts of each tappet together in a row, never mixed with another's: the body, socket and plunger are selectively fitted to give the right leak-down rate, which is the rate at which oil escapes past the plunger.

Take the tappet apart in order: the snap ring, the socket, the plunger, then the spring and the check-valve parts. Clean each part and inspect it. Nicks, scores and pitting are not allowed, and a plunger seized or scored means the whole tappet is discarded.

Why must the parts of one tappet never be swapped with those of another?
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (1980), Section XIII, paragraphs 13-1 to 13-3 (PDF pp. 84 and 85: a clean bench; unused solvent; each tappet's parts kept in a row so as not to interchange them, because bodies, sockets and plungers are selectively fitted to obtain the specified leak-down rate, the rate at which oil escapes past the plunger; disassembly order; inspection for nicks, scores, pitting and groove wear, none of which may be allowed; an entire assembly with a seized or scored plunger discarded) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 42 (a hydraulic tappet, Figure 1-30; normally adjusted at overhaul). The details belong to this manual; another engine's manual governs its own tappets.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The tappet kick-back test
steps.prompt:
A first check needs no special machine. Put together the plunger, the check-valve plate, the check-valve spring and the cage, without the large spring. Stand the dry body on its flat end and start the dry plunger into its bore.

With a screwdriver, push down on the bottom of the plunger with a short tap, and let go at once. The plunger should kick back promptly, because the air trapped under it is compressed. By repeated taps it can be pushed to the bottom as the air escapes.

A good kick-back means good compression: the tappet is acceptable, if nothing else is wrong. Rapid leakage may mean dirt on the check valve or its seat, or a worn plunger. Clean it again, and discard the tappet if it will not seat.

After the test, how should the inside of the body be coated when it is reassembled?
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (1980), Section XIII, paragraphs 13-4 and 13-5 (PDF p. 85: a quick check without special equipment, made immediately after cleaning; the dry plunger and valve assembly started into the dry body; the plunger pushed down with a screwdriver in a tapping motion and should kick back promptly because of the compression of trapped air; rapid leakage may be due to dirt on the check valve or seat, irregularities, or wear of the plunger; a tappet that cannot be made to seat is discarded; reassembly with only a film of clean engine oil in the body) and the special tools list, paragraph 5-10 (PDF p. 51: a valve lifter bleed-down tester to test the performance of hydraulic lifters accurately). The test is this manual's own; it is not a general rule for every engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Valves and springs: corrosion and wear
steps.prompt:
Look at each valve before you decide anything.

Examine the face and the tip for pitting and excessive wear. Minor pitting on a valve face can sometimes be removed by grinding.

Check for stretch. It shows as a smaller diameter of the stem near the neck, found with a micrometer or a valve radius gauge, and then check the stem's fit in its guide.

Use a magnifying glass on the stem area and the tip for cracks and nicks.

Look at the whole valve for damage from burning or corrosion, and do not reuse a valve that shows it.

Check each valve spring for cracks, rust, broken ends and compression.

Which of these could you find by eye alone?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 379 (using a magnifying glass, examine the valve in the stem area and the tip for cracks, nicks and other damage; examine the valve springs for cracks, rust, broken ends and compression) and PDF p. 380 (the face and tip should be examined for pitting and excessive wear, and minor pitting can sometimes be removed by grinding; inspect for stretch with a micrometer or a valve radius gauge, where stretch is a smaller diameter near the neck; measure the stem and check its fit in the guide; examine the valve for damage from burning or corrosion and do not re-use valves that indicate damage of this nature). The limits belong to the manufacturer's manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Checking a valve spring
steps.prompt:
A weak spring cannot close its valve firmly or hold it on its seat. A valve spring compression tester checks it.

The spring is compressed until its total height is the height the manufacturer specifies. The dial then shows, in pounds, the pressure needed to hold it there. That reading must lie within the manufacturer's limits.

For example, the GTSIO-520 manual's table of limits gives the outer valve spring, compressed to 1.275 inch, a serviceable limit of 118 lb, and 126 to 140 lb for a new one.

In the picture, find the spring, the dial and the height scale. What would you do with a spring that reads below its serviceable limit?
steps.alt: Photograph of a valve spring compression tester: a heavy cast base with a round dial at the front, a coil spring held between two plates in a vertical fixture above the dial, a small ruled scale beside the spring for reading its compressed height, and a long lever arm at the right.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 380 and 381 (compression is tested with a valve spring compression tester, Figure 10-15; the spring is compressed until its total height is that specified by the manufacturer; the dial indicates the pressure, in pounds, required to compress the spring to the specified height; this must be within the pressure limits established by the manufacturer). The example is from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Chapter B table of limits, March 1981, Spring Test Data (PDF p. 95: outer valve spring 637837 compressed to 1.275 inch, load 118 lb serviceable limit, 126 lb to 140 lb new parts); its own note says always to use the current data for the engine in front of you. The handbook does not say what to do with a spring below its limit; the lesson's answer, that it fails the test and is replaced, follows from the limit being a requirement.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook photograph shows a real tester, so the learner can name its parts before seeing the one in the workshop.

steps.title: Periodic exhaust checks
steps.prompt:
At each regular inspection, with the cowling off, look at every clamped connection and every port connection for leakage. Daily, check the exposed exhaust for cracks, scaling, excessive leakage and loose clamps.

A leak is usually two mated parts out of line. Loosen the clamps, reposition the parts, and tighten the nuts to no more than the specified torque. If that does not take up the looseness, the bolts and nuts have probably stretched: replace them, and safety the nuts.

Ceramic-coated stacks are cleaned by degreasing only. Parts hidden from view can be removed, plugged, pressurised to about 2 psi and put under water: bubbles show a leak. Never reuse an old gasket.

Why does a crack in a heat exchanger matter more than a crack in a stack?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 151 (the daily inspection of the exposed exhaust system for cracks, scaling, excessive leakage and loose clamps; each clamped and port connection inspected for leakage; an exhaust leak is usually poor alignment of two mated members; clamps loosened and parts repositioned; nuts retightened to no more than the specified torque, replaced if they do not tighten, since they have probably stretched, and safetied; ceramic-coated stacks cleaned by degreasing only; a component hidden or inaccessible removed, plugged, pressurised to about 2 psi and submerged in water) and PDF p. 152 (old gaskets never re-used; heat exchanger cracks let exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard). The Tanzanian regulation 31(6)(c) also lists exhaust stacks for cracks, defects and improper attachment.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The manual, the tools, the standard
steps.prompt:
Every task starts from the manufacturer's data. The maintenance or overhaul manual gives the order of work, the limits, the torque values and the special tools. The engine parts catalogue names the parts and gives their numbers.

The Tanzanian airworthiness regulations require the person doing maintenance to use the methods in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness, with the tools, equipment and test apparatus the work needs, and any special equipment the manufacturer recommends. The work must leave the aircraft or part at least equal to its original condition.

Keep the work clean and neat, protect openings, and use the proper tool. Why is a torque wrench specified for a cylinder hold-down nut, and not a spanner and a guess?
steps.note: Documented from the Tanzanian Civil Aviation (Airworthiness) Regulations, revised edition 2026, regulation 30(1) (maintenance by the methods, techniques and practices in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness, or others approved by the Authority; the tools, equipment and test apparatus necessary), 30(2) (special equipment recommended by the manufacturer) and 30(3) (the work must leave the aircraft or component at least equal to its original or properly altered condition), read from the TCAA website on 13 October 2026; the TCAA says its published copy is not authoritative; FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 409 (the engine parts catalog and its part numbers; neatness and cleanliness; improper torque on cylinder hold-down nuts can cause a cylinder malfunction and engine failure) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraphs 5-1 to 5-2 (PDF p. 51, special tools).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: What each practical asks of you
steps.prompt:
Practical A asks you to explain how the engine works, in order, while you watch or handle the training engine.

Practical B follows one pattern for every part: identify it, state its function, describe how it is built, and recognise a sign that it is not in good condition, relating that sign to the job the part does.

Practical C asks you to take part in the maintenance tasks safely, in the correct order and relationship, with the right tools and the maintenance information in front of you.

These are the outcomes your instructor wrote for the three practicals. Your instructor will tell you how the work is marked.

Which of the three do you feel least ready for?
steps.note: Documented from the instructor's three outcome lists for Practicals A, B and C and the Practical B note (identify it, state its function, describe its construction, recognise abnormal condition). The lesson states no marking scheme: the instructor has not supplied what the assessor looks for, and the instructor should confirm or add it.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Write one entry yourself
steps.prompt: Choose one part that you can name from the 3D steps, such as an accessory on the rear of the engine. Without looking at any worksheet, write the four things in your own words. Its full name. What it does, in one or two sentences. Its type, its material if you know it, and where it sits. And one thing you would look for to decide whether it is fit to fly, using a word from the list: corrosion, chafing, crack, dent or fretting. Then check your entry against the handbook. Where did your wording differ from it, and what does that tell you about what you still need to look up?
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the lesson (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) using the method set out in the student practical worksheets and the defect terms from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 371. The lesson does not supply answers for the worksheets; the learner's entries are their own.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner writes one entry in their own words.

checks.question: Put the steps of a complete overhaul in order.
checks.hint: Look before you clean, and measure before you rebuild.
items: Receiving inspection
Disassembly
Visual inspection
Cleaning
Structural inspection
Non-destructive testing
Dimensional inspection
Repair and replacement
Reassembly
Testing and break-in
checks.rationale: The handbook lists the ten steps in this order. The inspections are the most precise and most important phases, and visual inspection comes before cleaning so that the deposits are still there to be read.

checks.question: During a differential compression test, where do you hear air escaping for each leak?
checks.hint: Air takes the way out that is open to the leaking part.

pairs.right: At the exhaust outlet
At the air intake
At the crankcase breather

checks.rationale: Air that passes the exhaust valve goes out through the exhaust, air that passes the intake valve goes back out of the induction system, and air that passes the piston goes into the crankcase and out of the breather.

checks.question: Match each kind of storage to when it applies.
checks.hint: The limits are 30 days and 90 days.

pairs.right: Up to 30 days, after at least an hour of running
Not flown for 30 to 90 days
Over 90 days, or the engine is off the aircraft

checks.rationale: The handbook and the EASA text agree on 30 and 90 days. The course deck groups storage differently, as up to 30 days, one to six months and over six months, and the lesson follows the handbook.

checks.question: Match each dehydrator plug colour to what it tells you.
checks.hint: Cobalt chloride changes from blue towards white as moisture arrives.

pairs.right: Dry air, below 30 percent relative humidity
About 30 percent relative humidity
The plug has taken up moisture and needs attention
About 60 percent relative humidity

checks.rationale: Blue means little internal corrosion is expected. Lavender is about 30 percent, the pinks follow as humidity rises, and the plug is white at 60 percent. A plug that has changed colour is replaced, or dried if it is the kind that can be dried.

checks.question: To what regulated pressure is a differential compression tester set before the cylinder is tested?
checks.hint: It is the pressure of the air fed in through the orifice.
checks.rationale: The regulator is set to 80 psi. The gauge on the cylinder then shows how much of that pressure the cylinder holds, and a reading below the minimum for the engine means it is leaking.

checks.question: A cylinder hold-down nut is to be torqued to 500 inch-pounds. Your torque wrench reads in foot-pounds. What setting is that, to one decimal place?
checks.hint: There are 12 inches in a foot.
checks.rationale: 500 ÷ 12 = 41.7 foot-pounds. The GTSIO-520 manual's table gives 490 to 510 inch-pounds for these nuts, which is 40.8 to 42.5 foot-pounds.

checks.question: An engine has an overhaul life of 2,000 hours and has flown 500 hours. How many hours does it have left before overhaul?
checks.hint: Subtract the time flown from the life.
checks.rationale: 2,000 - 500 = 1,500 hours. This is the handbook's own example of time before overhaul. The manufacturer sets the life, and depending on how the engine is used the limit can be mandatory.

checks.question: Type I corrosion-preventive compound is a concentrate blended with three parts of oil to one part of concentrate. How many quarts of concentrate are in 8 quarts of the finished mixture?
checks.hint: The mixture is four parts in all.
checks.rationale: Three parts oil and one part concentrate make four parts, so one quarter of the mixture is concentrate: 2 quarts of concentrate with 6 quarts of oil. The mixture is blended separately and never made by adding concentrate to the oil already in the engine.

checks.question: When should a cylinder compression test be done on an engine that has been running?
checks.hint: Think about the condition of the rings and walls.
answers: After the engine has stood cold for a day
As soon as possible after shutdown, while the rings and walls are still oiled
Only after the spark plugs have been replaced
checks.rationale: A test straight after shutdown has the piston rings, cylinder walls and other parts freshly lubricated, so the reading is a true one. The ignition is off, and each plug is labelled to its cylinder.

checks.question: Why is the connecting rod supported as soon as a cylinder has been taken off?
checks.hint: Think about what the rod can hit.
answers: The rod falls and is damaged, or damages the crankcase
To stop the crankshaft turning
To keep oil from draining out of the engine
checks.rationale: With the cylinder and piston gone, nothing holds the rod. It can drop and strike the crankcase. The handbook supports each rod with the removed cylinder base seal ring looped around the rod and the studs.

checks.question: Why are engine parts not cleaned before the first visual inspection?
checks.hint: What is in the recesses?
answers: Cleaning would make the parts too hot to handle
Cleaning always damages the parts
Deposits of metal particles in the recesses can show how the failure began
checks.rationale: Residual metallic deposits in the recesses of the engine can be an indication of a failure, and cleaning removes them. Visual inspection comes first, then cleaning, then the structural and dimensional inspections.

checks.question: Why can repeated short ground runs of an engine in storage do more harm than good?
checks.hint: Water forms in the crankcase at every shutdown.
answers: The oil does not get hot enough for long enough to drive out the water, so water builds up in the oil and causes corrosion
They use up the preservative oil in the cylinders
They wear the piston rings faster than flying does
checks.rationale: Each shutdown leaves water vapour condensed in the crankcase. Only about 30 minutes at an oil temperature near 180°F purges it, and a ground run does not reach that, so the water accumulates.

checks.question: Why must the crankshaft not be turned after the final spraying of a preserved engine?
checks.hint: Think about the coating on the cylinder walls.
answers: The spark plugs would be shorted
The seal between the pistons and cylinder walls is broken and the coating is scraped off
The oil would drain from the sump
checks.rationale: Turning the engine breaks the seal of preservative between the pistons and the cylinder walls, so air can enter, and scrapes the coating off the walls so that bare metal is exposed. The engine carries a sign saying DO NOT TURN CRANKSHAFT and the date.

checks.question: According to the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, which parts are recommended for replacement at every major overhaul, whatever their condition?
checks.hint: Think about the parts in the valve train that work hardest.
answers: The crankshaft and camshaft
The exhaust valves, their rotocaps and the hydraulic valve lifters
The crankcase and the cylinder studs
checks.rationale: The manual's notes in paragraph 7-15 recommend replacing all exhaust valves and rotocaps, and all hydraulic lifters, at each major overhaul regardless of condition. Always read the current instructions for the engine in front of you.

checks.question: Under the Tanzanian airworthiness regulations, who must maintain an aircraft in an airworthy condition?
checks.hint: The duty is on the person who owns or uses the aircraft.
answers: The owner or operator of the aircraft
Only the engine manufacturer
Only the pilot, on each flight
Only the Authority
checks.rationale: Regulation 21 puts the duty on the owner or operator. An aircraft that is not maintained in an airworthy condition may not be operated until it is restored.

checks.question: Match each maintenance word to its meaning.
checks.hint: Two of them are about restoring, one is about examining and one is a small job.

pairs.right: Examining to establish that it conforms to an approved standard
Restoring to an airworthy condition after damage or wear
Restoring by disassembly, cleaning, inspection, repair as necessary and reassembly
Simple or minor preservation and replacing small standard parts

checks.rationale: These are the regulation's own meanings. Maintenance is the general word that includes overhaul, inspection, replacement, defect rectification and modifications or repairs.

checks.question: What must a person use when doing maintenance on an engine?
checks.hint: There is one first choice and one fallback.
answers: The current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness, or methods the Authority has approved if they are not available
Whatever method they remember from training
A general textbook
The course slides
checks.rationale: Regulation 30 requires the methods in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness, or Authority-approved methods where those are not available, with the special tools the manufacturer recommends.

checks.question: What does a service limit tell you about a part?
checks.hint: It is a limit on wear, not a nominal size.
answers: The most wear the part may have, or the least strength, and still be used
The size the part was when new
The number of hours the part has flown
The price of replacing the part
checks.rationale: A new part is made to a nominal size within a tolerance. A service limit is the point at which it must be repaired or replaced, as with the valve spring that is not reused below 73 lb.

checks.question: The manual allows a spark plug gap of 0.017 to 0.018 in. A plug measures 0.022 in. By how much is it over the largest allowed gap? Give the answer in inches.
checks.hint: Subtract the largest allowed gap from the measured gap.
checks.rationale: 0.022 - 0.018 = 0.004 in over the limit. A plug whose gap has eroded wider than the limit is not installed as it is: it is serviced and the gap set again, or replaced.

checks.question: A technician drops a spark plug on the hangar floor. What should be done?
checks.hint: Think about damage that cannot be seen.
answers: Discard it, because the shock can crack the insulator where it cannot be seen
Wipe it and fit it
Re-gap it and fit it
Fit it only on the lower side of the cylinder
checks.rationale: A plug that has been dropped on a hard surface should not be installed, because the shock usually causes small, invisible cracks in the insulator.

checks.question: Match each defect word to its meaning.
checks.hint: Each word names a different way for metal to be damaged.

pairs.right: Loss of metal by chemical action
Wear from two parts rubbing under light pressure
Surface damage from excessive heat
A partial separation of material, from vibration, overload or fatigue

checks.rationale: These are the handbook's definitions. Using the exact word in the record tells the next person what to look for.

checks.question: Metal particles are found on the oil filter element at an oil change. What does that suggest?
checks.hint: The metal came from inside the engine.
answers: Internal wear or a failing part, so the cause must be investigated and an overhaul may be indicated
Nothing, because oil always carries metal
That the filter is the wrong type
That the oil can simply be topped up
checks.rationale: The handbook says to check the oil and the filter for metal, and that when metal particles are found in the sump an overhaul of the engine is indicated.

checks.question: Which of these is preventive maintenance under the Tanzanian airworthiness regulations?
checks.hint: Preventive maintenance is simple or minor work.
answers: Replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap
Replacing a cylinder
A major overhaul
Replacing a crankshaft
checks.rationale: Regulation 29 lists replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the plug gap, and cleaning fuel and oil strainers, among the preventive maintenance. Who may do it is limited by regulation 26.

checks.question: What does the signature on a maintenance record entry approve?
checks.hint: It is limited to what was done.
answers: The return to service of the work performed, and no more
The return to service of the whole aircraft whatever else is wrong
The airworthiness of every engine of that type
The choice of a new overhaul period
checks.rationale: Regulation 42 says the signature constitutes the approval for return to service only for the work performed.

checks.question: For how many years after an engine is destroyed or permanently withdrawn from use must its log book be kept?
checks.hint: The regulation gives a number of years.
checks.rationale: Regulation 41 says every log book shall be preserved by the operator until two years after the aircraft, the engine or the propeller has been destroyed or permanently withdrawn from use.

checks.question: Which fuel grades does the GTSIO-520-H data page give?
checks.hint: Look at the first specification page.
answers: 100LL (blue) or 100 (green) aviation gasoline
Any automotive gasoline
80 octane aviation gasoline only
Jet fuel
checks.rationale: Page C-3-2 gives aviation grade fuel, 100LL (blue) or 100 (green). A lower grade in an engine that needs a high one can cause detonation.

checks.question: What is the maximum airspeed in level flight at maximum continuous power (VH) of a light-sport aircraft, in knots?
checks.hint: It is one of the limits that defines the category.
checks.rationale: VH may not be more than 120 knots calibrated airspeed under standard sea-level conditions. The stall speed limit is 45 knots and the maximum takeoff weight is 1,320 lb for an aircraft not intended for water.

checks.question: What is the maximum stall speed of a light-sport aircraft without lift-enhancing devices, in knots?
checks.hint: The handbook calls it VS1.
checks.rationale: The limit is 45 knots calibrated airspeed at maximum certificated takeoff weight and the most critical centre of gravity.

checks.question: A Rotax 914 has a TBO of 1,200 hours or 12 years, whichever comes first. The aircraft is flown 60 hours a year. After how many years must the engine be overhauled?
checks.hint: Work out how long 1,200 hours would take at 60 hours a year, then compare it with the calendar limit.
checks.rationale: 1,200 hours at 60 hours a year would take 20 years, so the 12-year calendar limit comes first. A seldom-flown engine is overhauled for its age, not its hours.

checks.question: In a leak-down test the input pressure is 80 psi and the cylinder gauge reads 60 psi. What is the percentage loss?
checks.hint: Loss = (input - reading) ÷ input.
checks.rationale: (80 - 60) ÷ 80 = 25 percent. The handbook gives a maximum allowable loss of 25 percent, and a differential lower than 80/60 indicates a problem.

checks.question: Match each person to what they may do.
checks.hint: Think about the rating and what it was trained for.

pairs.right: Preventive maintenance on a light-sport aircraft they own or operate
The annual condition inspection of an experimental aircraft they own
Maintenance, annual and 100-hour inspections of a special-certificate aircraft, and return to service
Maintenance and inspection of light-sport engines

checks.rationale: The inspection rating needs only a 16-hour course and is limited to the holder's own experimental aircraft. The maintenance rating needs a longer course, 120 hours for airplanes, and allows return to service. A sport pilot may only do preventive maintenance.

checks.question: Match each engine to its description.
checks.hint: Think about cycles, cylinders and cooling.

pairs.right: Two-cylinder, two-stroke inline engine, liquid-cooled
Four-stroke flat four with an exhaust-driven turbocharger
Air-cooled flat six of 120 hp
Four-cylinder carbureted engine of 100 hp

checks.rationale: The 582 is a liquid-cooled two-stroke. The 914 is a four-stroke flat four with liquid-cooled heads and a turbocharger. The Jabiru 3300 is a six-cylinder, ram-air-cooled engine, and the O-200 is a four-cylinder carbureted engine producing 100 bhp.

checks.question: Match each spark plug tip to what it tells you.
checks.hint: The plugs are taken out of a warm engine.

pairs.right: The plug is working correctly
The mixture is too rich
Too much oil in the chamber: check the rings and cylinder walls

checks.rationale: A light brown tip is healthy. Soot means a rich mixture, so check the choke, the air filter and the intake. Oil on the tip means oil is getting into the chamber past worn rings or cylinder walls.

checks.question: Which powered airplane could qualify as a light-sport aircraft?
checks.hint: Check seats, engines, propeller and landing gear.
answers: A two-seat airplane with one piston engine, a fixed-pitch propeller and fixed landing gear
A four-seat airplane with one piston engine and a fixed-pitch propeller
A two-seat airplane with two piston engines and fixed landing gear
checks.rationale: A light-sport aircraft has no more than two seats, a single reciprocating engine if powered, and a fixed or ground-adjustable propeller, with fixed gear except on water and glider types.

checks.question: When is the ignition of a light-sport engine live, even with the switch off?
checks.hint: Think about what the P-lead does.
answers: Only when the engine is hot
Whenever the ground lead is not properly connected to ground
Only when the battery is charged
checks.rationale: The handbook says that as long as the ground cable, the P-lead, is not properly connected to ground, the ignition is on. That is why the propeller is secured and a safety zone observed whenever the engine could be started.

checks.question: Knocking under load on a light-sport engine can be caused by:
checks.hint: Think back to detonation.
answers: Fuel of too low an octane rating, or fuel starvation giving a lean mixture
Too much oil in the sump
A propeller of too high a pitch
checks.rationale: Knocking under load is detonation. The handbook gives fuel with too low an octane rating, or fuel starvation and a lean mixture, as the causes, and the remedy is a higher octane fuel or checking the fuel supply.

checks.question: The cylinder head temperature goes above its maximum in flight. What does the handbook say to do?
checks.hint: Reduce the heat first, and then record it.
answers: Climb to cooler air and keep the power set
Reduce power to the minimum necessary, make a precautionary landing, and log the overage
Lean the mixture and continue to the destination
checks.rationale: Reduce engine power to the minimum necessary and carry out a precautionary landing. The pilot also enters the duration and extent of the over-temperature in the logbook.

checks.question: A significant amount of metal chips is found on the magnetic plug of a Rotax engine. What must be done?
checks.hint: The chips say something about the inside of the engine.
answers: Clean the plug and put it back
Change the oil only
The engine must be inspected, repaired or overhauled
checks.rationale: The magnetic plug reveals the internal condition of the gearbox and engine. A significant amount of chips means the engine must be inspected, repaired or overhauled. Only a few steel chips under about 3 mm can be tolerated.

checks.question: What kind of certificate of airworthiness may the Tanzanian Authority issue to a microlight or a kit-built aircraft that does not qualify for a normal one?
checks.hint: The certificate carries limits for each aircraft.
answers: A restricted certificate of airworthiness, with operating limitations and no international flights
A normal certificate with no limitations
No certificate at all: such aircraft cannot fly
A certificate for commercial air transport only
checks.rationale: Regulation 16 allows a restricted certificate of airworthiness for aircraft that do not qualify for one, including microlight, experimental amateur and kit built aircraft. It is subject to operating limitations in Tanzania, specific limits for each aircraft, and no international flights.

checks.question: Under the Tanzanian airworthiness regulations, when may a licensed pilot perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft?
checks.hint: There are three conditions: the aircraft, its use and the pilot's training.
answers: On an aircraft of 5,700 kg or less that the pilot owns or operates, that is not used by an air operator, and after a maintenance course on the type
On any aircraft, at any time
Only when no engineer is available
Only on an aircraft that is on an air operator's certificate
checks.rationale: Regulation 26(3) lets a licensed pilot perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft of 5,700 kg or less that the pilot owns or operates, not listed for use by an air operator, if the pilot has attended a maintenance course on the type.

checks.question: A licensed engineer is asked to sign for work on an engine type that is not entered on their licence. What do the licensing regulations say?
checks.hint: Privileges follow what is entered on the licence.
answers: The privileges may be exercised only for what is entered on the licence, so the engineer should not sign
Any licensed engineer may sign for any engine
The engineer may sign if the owner agrees
The engineer may sign if the work looks simple
checks.rationale: Regulation 127 allows the privileges to be exercised only in respect of the aircraft, powerplants and systems entered on the licence, with familiarity with the relevant information and recent experience.

checks.question: A licence holder must have at least how many months of experience in the preceding 24 months to exercise the privileges of an aircraft maintenance engineer licence?
checks.hint: The regulation gives a number of months.
checks.rationale: Regulation 127 requires that within the preceding 24 months the holder has had at least six months of experience in the inspection, servicing or maintenance of aircraft in accordance with the privileges, or has met the provisions for the issue of a licence.

checks.question: Put these in a sensible order for what to find out before working on a light aircraft.
checks.hint: Start with where the aircraft belongs and end with the job itself.
items: Where the aircraft is registered, and its authority
The certificate it holds, its category and limitations
The current manufacturer's data, directives and bulletins
What your licence allows you to sign
Whether the job is preventive maintenance, repair or overhaul
checks.rationale: The registration decides which authority's rules apply. The certificate and its limitations say what the aircraft may do. The data says how the work is done. Your licence says what you may sign, and the type of job decides who must inspect and sign.

checks.question: Why must an engineer find out the regulatory framework before doing maintenance on a recreational aircraft?
checks.hint: Think about what differs between categories and states.
answers: Maintenance privileges and permitted work can differ between categories of aircraft and between states
The rules are always the same everywhere
Recreational aircraft have no rules
Only the owner needs to know the rules
